events.descr: In the early 3rd millennium BCE Corded Ware peoples of marked steppe-related ancestry appear in Northern Europe; defensive palisades mark violent conflict between Funnelbeakers, Corded Ware and Pitted Ware. By 2650 BCE the Funnelbeaker culture has been replaced.

events.title: Yamnaya burial mounds over the Trypillian mega-sites
events.descr: Yamnaya tumuli dating to the middle of the 3rd millennium BC stand on top of Talianki and near Maidanetske.

source.sourceLocation: lead ('the middle of the 3rd millennium BC')

events.title: Biskupin fortified settlement built
events.descr: A Lusatian settlement of some 102–106 log houses inside a tall wooden palisade on an earth-and-timber rampart. Its oak was felled between 747 and 722 B.C., over half of it in the winter of 748/747.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, The site and Dating
infobox, lead, The site and Dating

events.title: Alexander the Great attacks the Getae
events.descr: On the lower Danube. Herodotus first used the name Getae; the Dacians were influenced by the Scythians and by the La Tène Celts who arrived in the 4th century BC.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Name and Origins and ethnogenesis
lead, Name and Origins and ethnogenesis

events.title: Old Copper complex: copper tools around the Great Lakes
events.descr: Widespread copper tools, weapons and ornaments, worked from 99% pure copper found near Lake Superior; by about 1,000 BCE copper is increasingly restricted to jewelry and status items. The Oconto site, with mostly flexed and bundle burials, was used between around 4,000 and 2,000 BCE.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Western Great Lakes and Oconto Site
lead, Western Great Lakes and Oconto Site

events.title: Indian Knoll shell midden
events.descr: Most heavily occupied in this period (the midden formed between 5500 and 2000 BC); trade reaches as far north as Lake Superior. By 1000 BC status differences show in grave goods.

sources.sourceLocation: Background, Burials and grave goods and Social complexity
Background, Burials and grave goods and Social complexity

events.title: Adena burial mounds
events.descr: Mounds built from hundreds of thousands of baskets of graded earth serve as burial and ceremonial sites; trade runs from Great Lakes copper to Gulf Coast shells. The Great Serpent Mound has been attributed to the culture, without conclusive evidence.

events.title: Paleo-Eskimo ancestors arrive from Siberia
events.descr: Genetic studies point to a single migration from Siberia around 4000 BC by the ancestors of the Saqqaq, Pre-Dorset and Dorset peoples.

events.title: The Saqqaq culture settles Greenland
events.descr: The longest-residing culture in Greenland’s history: small tents, seals, seabirds and other marine animals, and tools of silicified slate, agate, quartzite and rock crystal.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Timeframe and Archaeological findings
infobox, lead, Timeframe and Archaeological findings
infobox, lead, Timeframe and Archaeological findings

events.title: Independence I hunters in Greenland
events.descr: Muskoxen are a key part of their diet; microblades make up a large share of their tools. They disappear around 1900–1700 BC for unknown reasons.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, History and origin, Lifestyle and Tools
lead, History and origin, Lifestyle and Tools

events.title: The Dorset culture begins
events.descr: They hunt seals from holes in the ice and make soapstone lamps (qulliq) burning seal oil; unlike earlier cultures they lack bow and arrow.

events.title: Mokaya: the first pottery in Mesoamerica
events.descr: The Barra phase. A Mokaya site gives evidence of cacao beverages; the following Locona phase (1700–1500 BC) may have given the stimulus for the Gulf Olmec, and during the Cuadros period the area is believed to have come under Olmec hegemony.

sources.sourceLocation: Chronology, Barra, Locona and Ocós to Jocotal
Chronology, Barra, Locona and Ocós to Jocotal

events.title: San José Mogote, the first farming village of the Valley of Oaxaca
events.descr: Ceremonial buildings by 1300 B.C.; mirrors made here were traded to the Olmec Gulf Coast. Its dominance ends around 500 BCE with the rise of Monte Albán.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Development of civilization and Monument 3
infobox, lead, Development of civilization and Monument 3

events.title: Tlatilco chiefdoms in the Valley of Mexico
events.descr: Chiefdom centres at Tlatilco and Tlapacoya; Olmec-style objects are 'ubiquitous' in the earliest upper-middle status burials. By 700 BCE Cuicuilco is the largest city in the valley.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Defining the Tlatilco culture and Phases
lead, Defining the Tlatilco culture and Phases

events.title: Earliest Zapotec writing
events.descr: Monument 3 at San José Mogote carries the earliest Zapotec glyphs known, though its dating has been doubted. Zapotec writing is a predecessor of Maya, Mixtec and Aztec writing; whether Olmec symbols of 650 BC came first is debated.

source.sourceLocation: lead ('the first evidence of Zapotec hieroglyphic writing (600 B.C.)')
Technology ('the oldest Zapotec writing dated to about 500 BC')

events.title: Monte Albán founded
events.descr: Built on a mountaintop in a previously uninhabited no-man’s-land; about 5,200 people live there by around 300 BCE. The Danzantes carvings date from its earliest period and show traits of Olmec culture.

events.title: Kotosh: the Wairajirca period and first pottery
events.descr: One of three phases at Kotosh that preceded the Chavín culture; the earlier Mito period was preceramic.

sources.sourceLocation: Stratigraphy, Wairajirca period and Mito period
Stratigraphy, Wairajirca period and Mito period

events.title: Cupisnique adobe temples
events.descr: A distinctive adobe architecture; Cupisnique and Chavín share gods and artistic forms, and the Chavín built a temple beside Collud about three hundred years later. A mural of a spider god found in 2020 is about 3,200 years old.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Spider deity temple and Other Cupisnique sites
lead, Spider deity temple and Other Cupisnique sites

events.title: Paracas textiles and mummy bundles
events.descr: It makes significant contributions in the textile arts. Early Paracas communities were within the Chavín sphere, whose influence dwindled in 500–380 BCE; about 420 mummy bundles date to around 300–200 BCE, and the culture shows the earliest trepanations in the Americas.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Political and social organization, Mummy bundles and Trepanation
infobox, lead, Political and social organization, Mummy bundles and Trepanation

events.title: Earliest tattoo in the Americas (Chinchorro)
events.descr: The Chinchorro were famous for detailed mummification, practised from 7,000 BC; around 2000 BC their mummies change from black manganese to red.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Chinchorro mummies and Early tattoo
lead, Chinchorro mummies and Early tattoo

events.title: The Chinchorro culture ends
events.descr: Set around 3500 BP. Influences from the Andean Plateau lead to farming around 3,000 BP, and later groups no longer mummify their dead.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Chinchorro mummies and Later developments
lead, Chinchorro mummies and Later developments
lead, Chinchorro mummies and Later developments

events.title: The Casimiroid peoples
events.descr: They precede the Ortoiroid peoples.

events.title: Ortoiroid peoples move into the Antilles
events.descr: Known for stone tools but without ceramics; they bury their dead beneath shell middens. They settle Saint Kitts from 2000 BC to 400 BC and in many regions disappear by about 400 BC (the Coroso culture survives until 200 AD).

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Settlement patterns, Culture and Decline
lead, Settlement patterns, Culture and Decline

events.title: Saladoid potters reach the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico
events.descr: Farmers and potters living in settled villages, believed to have spoken an Arawakan language; they displace the pre-ceramic Ortoiroid culture.

events.title: Okunev stelae and the first bronze of north-eastern Central Asia
events.descr: The Okunev raise monumental stelae at gravesites and, with the neighbouring Samus culture, produce the first bronze in north-eastern Central Asia. Images of two-wheeled carts appear at the end of the 3rd millennium BC. They raise livestock, and closely interact with the successors of the Andronovo circle.

sources.sourceLocation: Dating, Monumental steles, Metallurgy, Wheeled transport, Livestock and Related cultures
Dating, Monumental steles, Metallurgy, Wheeled transport, Livestock and Related cultures

events.title: Glazkov hunters and fishers
events.descr: An economy of hunting, fishing and gathering, with copper knives and bronze fishing hooks; contemporary with the Andronovo culture to the west.

events.title: Ymyyakhtakh culture
events.descr: Bronze ware is frequent in its burial grounds; after 1,700 BC it is believed to spread east.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Description and Associated sites
infobox, lead, Description and Associated sites

events.title: Karasuk bronzes and chariots reach Shang China
events.descr: Karasuk farmers practise metallurgy on a large scale. Many Shang (13th–11th centuries BCE) and Zhou bronze blades derive from Karasuk designs, and Wu (2013) traces Shang chariots and their equipment to the Karasuk culture.

events.title: Deer stones raised in Mongolia
events.descr: Large standing stelae renowned for lively images of deer, part of a pastoral tradition of stone burial mounds; deer-stone art is earlier than the first Scythian sites such as Arzhan by 300 to 500 years. The oldest dated stones, in Khovsgol, are of about 1300 BC.

events.title: Slab-grave culture replaces the deer-stone culture
events.descr: In central and eastern Mongolia. The two cultures had been adjacent and essentially contemporaneous; slab-grave art shares many features with Karasuk and Tagar.

events.title: Tagar culture: royal kurgans and bronze-smelting
events.descr: One of the largest centres of bronze-smelting in ancient Eurasia. Huge royal kurgans are fenced by stone plaques with stelae at the corners; their animal art is very like that of the Scythians of southern European Russia. Usually considered descendants of the Andronovo culture.

events.title: Karuo: the first farmers on the Tibetan Plateau
events.descr: The oldest permanent settlement in Tibet and the earliest evidence for agriculture on the plateau, growing foxtail millet; its pottery resembles that of Majiayao sites. The residents abandon Karuo suddenly around 1750 BC.

events.title: Nyatri Tsenpo, first Yarlung king (traditional date)
events.descr: Some Tibetan texts give 126 BC, others 414 BC. Tibetan texts name the kingdom of Zhangzhung (c. 500 BC–625 AD) as the precursor of later Tibetan kingdoms.

events.title: Gandhara grave culture: the Swat graveyards
events.descr: Large graveyards appear in northern Gandhara close to the end of the second millennium BCE; the inhumations of c. 1200–900 BCE come from a period in which iron technology was introduced. Parpola links it with the Cemetery H culture in Punjab.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Location and Indo-Aryan migrations

source.sourceLocation: lead (no burials of this kind after 800 BCE)

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Location and Indo-Aryan migrations

events.title: Early Iron Age in South India
events.descr: Sites such as Hallur and Adichanallur are generally dated to around 1000 BCE; the Iron Age partly corresponds with the megalithic cultures of South India. Much earlier radiocarbon dates from Sivagalai and Mayiladumparai are disputed.

events.title: Sri Lankan cinnamon in Egypt
events.descr: Cinnamon, native to Sri Lanka, was in use in Ancient Egypt, suggesting trading links with the island.

events.title: A large settlement at Anuradhapura
events.descr: Founded before 900 BC at about 15 hectares, it expands to 50 ha within a couple of centuries. In the protohistoric period (1000–500 BCE) Sri Lanka is culturally united with southern India.

events.title: The African humid period ends: the Sahara dries
events.descr: Considered the greatest environmental transition of the Holocene in northern Africa; people move to places such as the Nile Valley and Mesopotamia, and the change is linked to the birth of Ancient Egyptian civilization. The end comes in several steps; by 2,700 years ago the central Sahara is a desert.

source.sourceLocation: End ('an ending date of 5,500 years before present is often used')

events.title: Pan-tropical drought about 4,000 years ago
events.descr: A major environmental change accompanied by the collapse of ancient civilizations and severe drought in Africa, Asia and the Middle East; some count this step (the 4.2-kiloyear event) as the true end of the humid period. Nile discharge decreases noticeably.

events.title: Herding reaches East Africa
events.descr: Livestock arrived in northern Africa around 8000 BP; as the Green Sahara dried, herders spread into the Nile Valley and reached the Turkana Basin around 5000 BP (3000 BC).

events.title: Herders reach the highlands of Kenya and Tanzania
events.descr: South Cushitic-speaking pastoralists who buried their dead in cairns settled first in the Kenyan lowlands (5,200–3,300 ybp). These early Cushitic speakers largely disappeared after the Bantu expansion.

events.title: First settlement of Palau
events.descr: Settled by Austronesian peoples, most likely from what is now the Philippines or Indonesia. The page’s history section places it between the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE.

source.sourceLocation: Early history ('between the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE')

events.title: Jericho, the first town
events.descr: Jericho is thought to be the world’s first town; it is the type site of the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A and B, defined by Kathleen Kenyon. PPNA people lived in tiny circular mud-brick dwellings, cultivated crops and hunted wild game, without pottery. The PPNA succeeds the Natufian culture.

events.title: The Tower of Jericho
events.descr: One of the world’s oldest towers and oldest stone buildings, built against the wall inside the town at the end of the PPNA; its construction is estimated to have taken 11,000 working days. Barkai and Liran suggest astronomical and social purposes.

events.title: Goats, sheep, pigs and cattle domesticated
events.descr: About 9000 BCE for goats and sheep, 8500 BCE for pigs and 8000 BCE for cattle. Çayönü is possibly the place where the pig was first domesticated.

events.title: Plastered skulls of the Levant
events.descr: Made in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic B, they are some of the oldest forms of art in the Middle East. In this period houses become rectilinear with thick white plaster floors; plaster work may have led to the discovery of pottery.

events.title: ’Ain Ghazal and its plaster statues
events.descr: At its prime around 7000 BCE some 3,000 people live here, four to five times contemporary Jericho. Its 32 plaster figures, some two-headed, are among the oldest large statues ever found. After 6500 BC the population drops to about one sixth.

events.title: The 8.2-kiloyear climate event
events.descr: Approximately 8,200 years before the present. At ’Ain Ghazal the population drops sharply after 6500 BC, a decline its page links to this event.

events.title: Ghassulian villages: copper and painted walls
events.descr: Mixed farming hamlets with remarkable polychrome wall paintings (including the "Ghassulian Star"); they smelted copper and buried their dead in stone dolmens. The culture correlates closely with the Amratian of Egypt.

events.title: Göbekli Tepe: circular enclosures with stone pillars
events.descr: Popularly called the world’s first temples: at least 20 large enclosures with stone pillars, carved with reliefs of animals, built by hunter-gatherers who supplemented their diet with early domesticated cereal. The earliest exposed structures date to 9500–9000 BCE. Karahan Tepe and other nearby sites share its architecture and iconography.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Dawn of village life and Chronology
infobox, lead, Dawn of village life and Chronology

events.title: Copper and malachite workshop at Çayönü
events.descr: A specialised workshop found in 2026. Çayönü belongs to the Taş Tepeler tradition of Göbekli Tepe and is an early example of agriculture, implemented from the 9th millennium BC.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Archaeology and Origin of domestication
lead, Archaeology and Origin of domestication

events.title: Çatalhöyük
events.descr: A settlement of domestic buildings with no obvious public buildings, with 18 successive layers of buildings and flourishing around 7000 BC. Ornate murals in some of the larger rooms include what is frequently cited as the world’s oldest map; over 2,500 clay figurines have been found, and some skulls were plastered and painted. About 600–800 people lived there in an average year of the middle phase (6700–6500 BC).

events.title: Hassuna: the first farmers of northern Mesopotamia
events.descr: By around 6000 BC people had moved into the foothills of northernmost Mesopotamia, making cream-slipped pottery painted in red; Umm Dabaghiyah is believed to have the region’s earliest pottery.

events.title: Halaf culture: painted pottery and the first stamp seals
events.descr: The earliest systematic plant motifs in Near Eastern prehistoric art and the earliest known stamp seals in the Near East; Halaf-influenced material is found throughout Greater Mesopotamia. Most scholars see its end as a Halafian adoption of the Ubaid culture.

events.title: Samarra culture: early irrigation
events.descr: Irrigation and flax at Tell es-Sawwan show a prosperous settled culture; it is best known for fine pottery decorated with stylised animals, and was the precursor of the Ubaid period.

events.title: Tell el-’Oueili: the oldest known site in southern Mesopotamia
events.descr: Its Ubaid 0 levels are older than those of Eridu. The earliest settlements south of Uruk date to the eighth millennium BC.

source.sourceLocation: Climate ('the Ubaid 0 levels at Oueili (6500-6000 BC)')

events.title: Eridu founded
events.descr: Built on a virgin sand dune, it was traditionally the earliest city of southern Mesopotamia in the Sumerian King List. Eighteen superimposed mudbrick temples stand at the site, and twelve clay tokens from its Ubaid levels are precursors of proto-cuneiform.

events.title: Chogha Golan: domesticated emmer wheat
events.descr: The earliest record of long-term plant management in Iran: people lived mainly on wild plants and hunting, and domesticated emmer appears about 2,000 years after wild barley is first found (around 9,800 BP).

events.title: Ganj Dareh: the earliest domesticated goats
events.descr: The earliest evidence for goat domestication in the world; two-row barley is the only domesticated crop found so far.

events.title: Jeitun: the oldest arable farming in Central Asia
events.descr: Villagers kept sheep and goats that were already domesticated, and built with sun-dried clay blocks. The culture may have begun before 7000 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Jeitun culture, Agriculture and Excavations
lead, Jeitun culture, Agriculture and Excavations

events.title: Chogha Mish settled
events.descr: Its Early Susiana period is contemporary with Ubaid 1 in southern Mesopotamia. The main monumental building is destroyed in the early 5th millennium BC, and the site declines about 4400 BC.

events.title: Tepe Sialk settled
events.descr: Tombs of Sialk I contain pottery. Later, silver metallurgy at the site is radiocarbon-dated to 3660–3520 B.C., and Sialk IV has links with Uruk-period Mesopotamia and with Proto-Elamite Susa.

sources.sourceLocation: History, Sialk I, Sialk IV and Silver metallurgy
History, Sialk I, Sialk IV and Silver metallurgy

events.title: Shahr-e Sukhteh founded
events.descr: In Period I it has connections with the Proto-Elamite cities of Khuzestan and Fars; later it is in contact with the pre-Harappan centres of the Indus valley.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, Archaeology, Period I and Period II
infobox, Archaeology, Period I and Period II

events.title: Shulaveri–Shomu: the earliest winemaking
events.descr: The earliest evidence for winemaking and grape cultivation in the Near East. Goats, sheep, cows, pigs and dogs are kept from the earliest phase; around 5900 BC villagers at Gadachrili attempt to divert the Shulaveri river to nearby fields, the oldest water management in the Caucasus.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Subsistence and Earliest grapes
infobox, lead, Subsistence and Earliest grapes

events.title: Nabta Playa: herders and early pottery
events.descr: One of the earliest sites of the Nubian Neolithic. People begin to make pottery locally around 6800 BC, and larger settlements appear by the 7th millennium BC; domesticated cattle reach northeast Africa in the late 7th millennium BC.

events.title: Nabta Playa stone circle
events.descr: May be among the world’s earliest known archaeoastronomical devices; a megalith period follows, about 4500 to 3600 BC. Researchers see the site as an early evolution of the Hathor cult.

sources.sourceLocation: Astronomical observation, Recent research and Religious ties
Astronomical observation, Recent research and Religious ties

events.title: Faiyum A: the earliest farming culture in the Nile Valley
events.descr: Weaving is evidenced for the first time; goats and sheep had been introduced from the Neolithic Levant around 6000 BCE. Neolithic settlements appear all over Egypt from around 6210 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: Faiyum A culture and Neolithic anthropology
Faiyum A culture and Neolithic anthropology

events.title: Merimde culture
events.descr: Cattle, sheep, goats and pigs are kept; its later phase corresponds to the Faiyum A and Badari cultures.

events.title: Badarian culture: the earliest farming in Upper Egypt
events.descr: They keep cattle, sheep and goats, give livestock and dogs ceremonial burial, and make black-topped pottery; the Western Desert was probably the most influential of its sources.

source.sourceLocation: lead ('might have already emerged by 5000 BC')

events.title: Naqada I (Amratian)
events.descr: Obsidian and a little gold are imported from Nubia, and charcoal from Nekhen tombs is cedar from Lebanon. Werner Kaiser’s chronology starts the Naqada culture c. 4000 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead and Commerce and crafts

events.title: Capsian hunters of Algeria and Tunisia
events.descr: An Epipalaeolithic tradition whose first phase overlaps the African humid period, in open savanna; they hunted game from aurochs and hartebeest to hares and snails. Historical linguists tentatively link it with the earliest Afroasiatic speakers in Africa.

events.title: Gobero: the oldest cemetery in the Sahara
events.descr: Kiffian fisher-gatherers, makers of pottery with wavy lines, live beside a large lake in the Green Sahara (7500–3500 BCE); after a gap (6200–5200 BCE) Tenerian people herd domesticated cattle there. At least 182 burials include a man buried with a turtle carapace and a grave decorated with flowers.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Site, Excavations, Kiffian culture, Tenerian culture and Burials
infobox, lead, Site, Excavations, Kiffian culture, Tenerian culture and Burials

events.title: The Dufuna canoe, Africa’s oldest boat
events.descr: The second-oldest known boat in the world, after the Pesse canoe.

events.title: Star Carr
events.descr: Britain’s oldest structure and the earliest known carpentry in Europe; a pendant found in 2015 is thought to be the oldest Mesolithic art in Britain. Occupation lasts about 800 years.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Settlement and artefacts and Post-2000 investigations
infobox, lead, Settlement and artefacts and Post-2000 investigations

events.title: Maglemosian culture of Northern Europe
events.descr: They appear to have domesticated the dog; bark huts survive, and the leister, a characteristic type of fishing spear, is typical of the culture.

events.title: Lepenski Vir: fish-faced sculptures
events.descr: The late architectural phase, with numerous fish sculptures with human-like faces. From about 7500 BC Early European Farmers arriving from Asia Minor begin to settle the Balkans and the Danube valley.

events.title: Farming reaches Greece
events.descr: Neolithic material culture came to Europe via western Anatolia. Farming spread from the Aegean to Britain in about 2,500 years (6500–4000 BC), at about 1 km a year; the Sesklo culture is called the earliest known Neolithic culture of Europe.

events.title: Starčevo–Körös–Criș farmers
events.descr: Dated by the infobox; the body gives about 5500–4500, and other sources 6200–5200.

events.title: Cardial Ware farmers spread along the Mediterranean
events.descr: Pottery impressed with cockle shells, from Epirus and Corfu (6400–6200 BC) to the Atlantic coasts of Portugal and Morocco; it spreads about 2,000 km, from the Gulf of Genoa to the Mondego estuary, in probably no more than 100–200 years. Its people were closely related to the earlier Neolithic farmers of north-west Anatolia.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, The Mediterranean Neolithic and Genetics
infobox, lead, The Mediterranean Neolithic and Genetics

events.title: Linear Pottery farmers spread across central Europe
events.descr: Appearing about 5600–5400 BC on the middle Danube, the culture spreads about 1,500 km in 360 years, building long houses.

events.title: Vinča culture: early copper smelting and Vinča symbols
events.descr: It has the earliest known example of copper smelting, and its symbols are conjectured by some to be the earliest proto-writing.

events.title: Varna Necropolis: the oldest gold
events.descr: The oldest gold treasure and jewellery in the world, dated by radiocarbon in 2006.

events.title: The Carnac stones
events.descr: A dense collection of megalithic sites near the south coast of Brittany; the tumulus at Tumiac was raised between 4790 and 4530 BC, contemporary with the rich Varna burials.

events.title: Mehrgarh: the earliest farming in South Asia
events.descr: A farming village of unbaked mud brick; barley and zebu cattle were probably domesticated locally, and drilled teeth show proto-dentistry. Its dating is debated (Jarrige: before 7000 BCE; Mutin and Zazzo: 5250–4650 BCE). Its culture later migrated into the Indus Valley and became the Indus Valley Civilisation.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Period I, Lifestyle, History and Notes
lead, Period I, Lifestyle, History and Notes

events.title: Bhirrana’s earliest levels (Hakra ware)
events.descr: Charcoal from the lowest levels gave 7570–7180 BCE, said to predate the Indus Valley civilisation; a review by Garge gives a 'tentative chronological bracket' of '6000(?)-4600-3800' for the lowermost levels.

events.title: Lahuradewa: early rice and pottery in the Ganges plain
events.descr: Rice from Period IA is AMS-dated to the 7th millennium BCE, but whether it was cultivated or gathered wild is debated; its pottery is the oldest evidence of ceramics in the Indian Subcontinent. Irfan Habib gives 4220–2879 BCE.

events.title: Domesticated rice at Pengtoushan
events.descr: Rice residues carbon-dated to 8200–7800 BC show that rice had been domesticated; by 4000 BC evidence of rice domestication in the region is abundant.

events.title: Jiahu: bone flutes, carved signs and fermented drink
events.descr: The earliest Peiligang site: 33 flutes carved from crane wing bones, eleven pictographic symbols on tortoise shell and bone, foxtail millet and rice, alcohol fermented from rice, honey, grapes and hawthorn, and the earliest common-carp aquaculture. A flood ends it around 5700 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Inscriptions, Agriculture and Pottery and alcohol production
infobox, lead, Inscriptions, Agriculture and Pottery and alcohol production

events.title: Peiligang millet farmers
events.descr: Cultivating millet and raising pigs, they make some of the oldest pottery in ancient China; their society is egalitarian. They are followed by the Yangshao culture.

events.title: Xinglongwa: the earliest discovered ditched site in China
events.descr: Houses built in rows; 120 pit-houses at Xinglongwa. In the richest grave a man is buried with a pair of pigs and jade objects, and millet remains are found.

events.title: Hemudu: stilt houses and early rice
events.descr: One of the earliest rice-growing cultures; its people live in long stilt houses and make black pottery, carved jade, ivory, bone whistles and a red lacquer bowl.

events.title: Yangshao painted pottery (Banpo phase)
events.descr: Millet farmers who also grow some rice and raise pigs; they make white, red and black painted pottery. A dragon statue of the fifth millennium BC is the world’s oldest known dragon depiction. Scholars trace a line from Yangshao to the Longshan and Shang cultures.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Phases, Origins, Subsistence, Crafts and Social structure
infobox, lead, Phases, Origins, Subsistence, Crafts and Social structure

events.title: Hongshan jade dragons
events.descr: Known for jade pig dragons and embryo dragons, among the earliest jade working; it interacts with the contemporary Yangshao, and its jades show considerable kinship with some Shang jades.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Historical context, Artifacts and Development of Chinese civilization
infobox, lead, Historical context, Artifacts and Development of Chinese civilization

events.title: Dawenkou culture
events.descr: Turquoise, jade and ivory are common; the earliest alligator drums appear here. It co-exists with the Yangshao culture and sometimes has the lead role, notably in generating Longshan.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Chronology and Interactions with other cultures
infobox, lead, Chronology and Interactions with other cultures

events.title: Early Jeulmun pit-house villages
events.descr: Small semi-permanent settlements with pit-houses. Gosan-ni pottery has been dated to 10,000 BC, though more dating is needed.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Incipient Jeulmun and Early Jeulmun
infobox, lead, Incipient Jeulmun and Early Jeulmun

events.title: Domesticated peaches reach Jōmon Japan from China
events.descr: In the Early Jōmon, a period that saw an explosion in population. Jōmon pottery, decorated by impressing cords into wet clay, is among the oldest in the world.

sources.sourceLocation: Chronology, Early Jōmon, Early agriculture and Pottery
Chronology, Early Jōmon, Early agriculture and Pottery

events.title: Kuk Swamp: drainage ditches and early agriculture
events.descr: One of the places where people independently developed agriculture; taro was grown, and drainage ditches date back to about 9,000 years ago.

events.title: Bananas and sugar cane planted at Kuk
events.descr: Eumusa bananas; a managed grassland of 6950–6550 years ago points to deliberate planting.

events.title: Plano bison hunters
events.descr: They hunted Bison antiquus, forcing stampedes off cliffs.

events.title: The oldest dogs in the Americas (Koster)
events.descr: Dog burials about 9,900 years old at one of the oldest known cemetery sites in eastern North America, occupied from the early Archaic (7500 BC).

events.title: Windover pond burials
events.descr: Hunter-gatherers bury their dead in the pond; brain tissue survives in 91 skulls, and graves hold woven palm-leaf fabrics and the earliest documented bottle gourd north of Mexico.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Site, Deposition, Textiles and Bags and containers
lead, Site, Deposition, Textiles and Bags and containers

events.title: Squash domesticated at Guilá Naquitz
events.descr: The earliest known evidence for domestication of any crop on the continent: intentional breeding of squash (C. pepo) by no later than 8,000 years BP. Earlier AMS dates of 10,000 BP have been called into question.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Crop domestication and Timeline of domesticate changes

source.sourceLocation: Crop domestication ('no later than 8,000 years BP')

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Crop domestication and Timeline of domesticate changes

events.title: Maize domesticated in southern Mexico
events.descr: Domesticated by indigenous peoples from wild teosinte about 9,000 years ago.

events.title: Cueva de las Manos: the oldest-known cave paintings in South America
events.descr: The oldest-known cave paintings in South America, made in several waves until AD 700 by hunters of guanacos.

events.title: Potatoes domesticated around Lake Titicaca
events.descr: In southern Peru and northwestern Bolivia, about 7,000–10,000 years ago.

events.title: Paloma, one of the earliest villages in the Americas
events.descr: One of the earliest villages in the Americas dated stratigraphically; its diet was mainly fish and shellfish.

events.title: Huaca Prieta: early maize and dyed cotton
events.descr: Corncobs from Paredones and Huaca Prieta may date from as early as 4700 BCE (Dolores Piperno); dyed cotton fabric found in 2016 is about 6000 years old.

sources.sourceLocation: Early maize found and Early use of cotton and indigo dye
Early maize found and Early use of cotton and indigo dye

events.title: Karahan Tepe
events.descr: Possibly the earliest known human village. It lies in the same region as Göbekli Tepe, predates its construction by several centuries, and archaeologists believe the sites are related.

events.title: Nevalı Çori: temples and monumental sculpture
events.descr: Some of the world’s oldest known temples and monumental sculpture, in the Taş Tepeler tradition; similar structures are known only from Göbekli Tepe.

events.title: Aşıklı Höyük settled
events.descr: One of the earliest Aceramic Neolithic sites on the Anatolian plateau, considerably smaller than nearby Çatalhöyük.

events.title: Abu Hureyra: a farming village on the Euphrates
events.descr: One of the most important sites in the study of the origins of agriculture; its first domesticated cereals came about around 10,000 years ago, and basket weaving there dates back to 6500 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Second occupation, Transition from foraging to farming and Agriculture
lead, Second occupation, Transition from foraging to farming and Agriculture

events.title: Byblos first settled
events.descr: In the Pre-Pottery Neolithic B; Byblos has been continuously inhabited since 5000 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and Neolithic and Chalcolithic levels
lead and Neolithic and Chalcolithic levels

events.title: Yarmukian culture
events.descr: A Pottery Neolithic A culture of the Levant, existing alongside the Lodian (Jericho IX) and Nizzanim cultures.

events.title: Jarmo, an early farming village
events.descr: An agricultural community contemporary with Jericho and Çatalhöyük, at its height between 6200 and 5800 BC; its art marks the inception of the Art of Mesopotamia.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, The village and Pottery and religion
infobox, lead, The village and Pottery and religion

events.title: Tell Brak settled
events.descr: The earliest small settlement belongs to the proto-Halaf culture; Halaf and Northern Ubaid phases follow.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, history table and Early settlement
infobox, lead, history table and Early settlement
infobox, lead, history table and Early settlement

events.title: Tell Brak becomes one of the first cities
events.descr: Urbanisation begins in the late 5th millennium BCE; in Period E (c. 4200–3900 BC) the city’s walls are built, and by early Period F (c. 3800–3600 BC) it covers 130 hectares. It is one of the earliest known cities in the world; later an Urukean colony is established there.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Brak Period E and Brak Period F
lead, Brak Period E and Brak Period F

events.title: Ounjougou: the earliest pottery in Africa
events.descr: Before 9400 BCE Niger-Congo speakers independently created and used mature ceramic technology; the pottery makers later migrate, and pottery at Bir Kiseiba in Egypt resembles Ounjougou’s.

source.sourceLocation: Early Holocene ('during the first half of the 10th millennium BC')

events.title: Early Khartoum pottery makers
events.descr: From a time before food production began in Africa; sites in Sudan such as Esh Shaheinab are some of the earliest examples of pottery-making in Africa.

sources.sourceLocation: lead ('Early Khartoum (8800 to 5000 BP)') and Pottery
lead ('Early Khartoum (8800 to 5000 BP)') and Pottery

events.title: The Pesse canoe, the world’s oldest known boat
events.descr: Made in the early Mesolithic.

events.title: Doggerland floods: Britain is cut off
events.descr: Rising seas inundate Doggerland between 10,000 and 7,000 years ago, cutting the British peninsula off from the mainland by around 6500 BCE; Dogger Bank remains an island until at least 5000 BCE. Doggerland may have been Europe’s most prosperous hunting, fowling and fishing ground in the Mesolithic.

events.title: The Storegga Slide tsunami
events.descr: Structural failures of the continental shelf cause underwater landslides and a tsunami in the North Atlantic; one hypothesis holds that it flooded much of Doggerland’s remaining coast.

events.title: Ertebølle hunter-fishers make pottery
events.descr: A hunter-gatherer and fisher culture of the end of the Mesolithic, roughly contemporary with the Linear Pottery culture; shortly after 4,100 BCE it spreads along the Baltic coast, and it is then replaced by the Funnelbeaker culture.

events.title: Hamangia culture: “The Thinker”
events.descr: Known for exceptional clay figures, including The Thinker and Sitting Woman (c. 4900 BC); it is followed by the Varna culture.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, Genesis and successor, Art and Gallery
infobox, Genesis and successor, Art and Gallery

events.title: Dimini culture: abstract painted vessels
events.descr: Characteristic of the Later Neolithic in eastern Thessaly. An "invasion theory" has it conquering the Sesklo culture around 5000 BC; Lyritzis’s thermoluminescence dates instead show it appearing about 4800 BC, four centuries before Sesklo’s end.

events.title: The Goseck circle
events.descr: Perhaps the oldest and best known of the circular enclosures of the Central European Neolithic, presented as a ritual or cult structure; it dates to the transition from Linear Pottery to Stroke-ornamented ware.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, History and Astronomical alignment
infobox, lead, History and Astronomical alignment

events.title: Lengyel culture: the dawn of the Chalcolithic in Central Europe
events.descr: Copper beads and ribbons mark the dawn of the Chalcolithic in Central Europe. It follows the Linear Pottery culture and overlaps the Funnelbeaker culture.

events.title: Michelsberg culture
events.descr: Undecorated tulip beakers, hilltop settlements and enclosures; it emerges in northeastern France and plays an instrumental role in establishing the Funnelbeaker culture. Its Kapellenberg tumulus shows the influence of the Castellic culture of Brittany.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, History, Settlements and Finds
infobox, lead, History, Settlements and Finds

events.title: Barnenez cairn
events.descr: One of the earliest megalithic monuments in Europe, remarkable for its megalithic art; built in two phases (4850–4250 and 4450–4000 BC).

events.title: Knap of Howar, the oldest stone house in northern Europe
events.descr: It may be the oldest preserved stone house in northern Europe, earlier than the similar houses at Skara Brae.

events.title: Bacsonian culture
events.descr: Often regarded as a variation of the Hoabinhian, a lithic techno-complex. At Spirit Cave in Thailand, Gorman claimed early plant remains, but Higham and Thosarat find no grounds for linking the site with agriculture; it has no ceramics until after 6800 BCE (Solheim).

sources.sourceLocation: lead and Hoabinhian and plant domestication
lead and Hoabinhian and plant domestication

events.title: Cishan millet farmers
events.descr: Farming of broomcorn millet, stored in over 500 pits; pigs are the main source of meat, and nets are made of hemp. Dates of 10,000 years ago for its millet have been questioned. It is followed by the Yangshao culture.

events.title: Houli culture in Shandong
events.descr: Rice, broomcorn millet and foxtail millet are found at its sites (rice at Yuezhang AMS-dated to 8010–7700 BP, not confirmed as domesticated); people live in square semi-subterranean houses and rely mostly on hunting and fishing.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Archaeological findings and Yuezhang
infobox, lead, Archaeological findings and Yuezhang

events.title: Daxi culture: rice and walled settlements
events.descr: The Daxi people cultivate rice extensively, and their sites are some of the earliest in China with moats and walled settlements.

events.title: Majiabang culture: paddy rice and jade
events.descr: Paddy fields at Caoxieshan and Chuodun; jade ornaments, and a wooden scull and oar. It coexists with the Hemudu culture and is succeeded by the Liangzhu culture.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Rice cultivation, Tools, Jade and Related cultures
infobox, lead, Rice cultivation, Tools, Jade and Related cultures

events.title: Caverna da Pedra Pintada: the earliest cave paintings in the Americas
events.descr: Human presence about 11,200 to 10,000 years ago, with spear points and Brazil nuts; its paintings are the earliest known cave paintings in the Americas.

events.title: The Spirit Cave mummy
events.descr: The oldest human mummy found in North America, wrapped in a rabbit-skin blanket and woven tule matting.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Discovery and Identity and dating
infobox, lead, Discovery and Identity and dating

events.title: Almendres Cromlech
events.descr: Its construction dates back to the 6th millennium BC, in three phases: Almendres I (6000 BC, Early Neolithic), II (5000 BC) and III (4000 BC).

events.title: The first farmers reach Iberia
events.descr: In the 6th millennium BC the first agriculturalists arrive in Andalusia, and Cardium pottery culture reaches eastern Iberia.

events.title: The first dolmens, in southern Portugal
events.descr: Possibly the oldest dolmen tombs of their kind anywhere.

events.title: The Dolmen of Menga (Antequera)
events.descr: The Antequera Dolmens date from after c. 3700 BC.

events.title: Kuahuqiao: an early dugout canoe and paddy rice
events.descr: A very early dugout canoe, the earliest technology of its kind in China, and paddy rice cultivated 7700 years ago; villagers had domesticated rice, dogs and pigs. Rising seas may have suddenly deluged the area around 7,550 years ago.

events.title: Budj Bim eel traps
events.descr: Carbon-dated to 6,600 years old.

events.title: Sanganakallu Neolithic settlement
events.descr: A Neolithic site.

events.title: Round Head rock art period in the Sahara
events.descr: One of the periods of Saharan rock art (9500–7000 BP), after the Large Wild Fauna and Kel Essuf periods.

events.title: Pastoral period of Saharan rock art
events.descr: Dated 7200–3000 BP. In Egypt, the Cave of Beasts was painted by people who lived between c. 6500 and 4400 BCE.

sources.sourceLocation: Rock art time periods and Archaeological sites
Rock art time periods and Archaeological sites

events.title: Horse period of Saharan rock art
events.descr: Dated 3200–1000 BP; the Camel Period follows (3000–2000 BP).

events.title: Wilton culture: small stone tools
events.descr: A shift from large to small stone technology, 8,000 to 4,000 years ago; at Nelson Bay Cave people depended on small game from 9,000 to 5,000 years ago. Janette Deacon identifies a mature phase around 4,800 years ago.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, History, Stone technology and Diet
lead, History, Stone technology and Diet

events.title: Kintampo complex
events.descr: Established by Saharan agropastoralists; pearl millet spreads into the West African savanna after 2500 cal BC (Champion et al. 2022), and oil palm use starts at least 4000 years ago. Watson dates its appearance to 3,600–3,200 bp.

events.title: Las Vegas culture of coastal Ecuador
events.descr: One of the oldest cultures in the Americas, on the Santa Elena Peninsula; at approximately 6000 BC it is among the first to begin farming (bottle gourd and early maize). Its best-known remains are the Lovers of Sumpa.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and Preceramic period > Las Vegas culture
lead and Preceramic period > Las Vegas culture

events.title: Oshara tradition: the Jay phase
events.descr: A Southwestern Archaic tradition. The Jay phase (7,450 to 6,750 years before present) is followed by the Bajada and San Jose phases.

events.title: Maize cultivation begins in the Oshara tradition
events.descr: The Armijo phase (3,750 to 2,750 years BP).

events.title: The Basketmaker culture begins
events.descr: It continues until about 750 CE.

events.title: San Pedro phase of the Cochise tradition
events.descr: The southern of the four Southwestern Archaic traditions; provisional radiocarbon dates.

events.title: Eannatum of Lagash defeats Umma: the Stele of the Vultures
events.descr: The earliest known war monument. Eannatum established one of the first verifiable empires in history, subduing Elam and destroying Susa.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead and Stele of the Vultures
infobox, lead and Stele of the Vultures

events.title: Urukagina of Lagash
events.descr: King of Lagash and Girsu, described by one study as the first social reformer in history, though there is no solid evidence for a single "reform of Urukagina".

events.title: Gudea of Lagash
events.descr: Best known for the many statues of him; about 600 tablets survive from his dynasty. Exactly when in the 22nd century BC he reigned cannot be determined.

events.title: The Epic of Gilgamesh (Old Babylonian version)
events.descr: The world’s oldest surviving narrative literature. Sumerian Gilgamesh poems may date to the Third Dynasty of Ur (c. 2100 BCE); the Standard Babylonian version was compiled by Sîn-lēqi-unninni between 1300 and 1000 BCE.

events.title: Tushratta of Mitanni
events.descr: King of Mitanni at the end of the reign of Amenhotep III, to whom he wrote letters.

events.title: Hazor, the great Canaanite city, burns
events.descr: A stratum from around 1200 BCE (13th century) shows catastrophic fire and a scorched palace; the cause is disputed. Hazor had been a major city since the Middle Bronze Age (around 1750 BCE).

events.title: Assyria captures Hazor
events.descr: Despite its defences the city is captured and its population deported.

events.title: The Library of Ashurbanipal
events.descr: More than 30,000 clay tablets and fragments from the 7th century BCE, among them the Epic of Gilgamesh. Nineveh is destroyed in 612 BCE.

events.title: Exiles return from Babylon
events.descr: After the deportations of 597, 587 and 582 BCE, the exiled Judeans are permitted by the Persians to return after the Battle of Opis; the Second Temple is begun c. 537 BCE.

events.title: The Cyrus Cylinder
events.descr: An Achaemenid royal inscription in the name of Cyrus the Great, made after the Persian conquest of Babylon; the British Museum dates it between 539 and 530 BC.

events.title: Persepolis built
events.descr: The ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire. Cyrus may have chosen the site, but Darius I built the terrace and palaces (André Godard); a broad stairway was begun around 519 BC.

events.title: Zoroaster (date unknown)
events.descr: An Iranian religious reformer. There is no consensus on his date: many scholars consider around 1000 BC most likely, others a range of 1500 to 500 BC; tradition places him in the 7th and 6th centuries BC.

events.title: The Iliad and the Odyssey
events.descr: Traditionally credited to Homer; the poems are thought to have been composed around the late eighth or early seventh century BC.

source.sourceLocation: lead ('the late eighth or early seventh century BC')

events.title: Hesiod’s Works and Days
events.descr: Hesiod is generally thought to have been active between 750 and 650 BC; Works and Days describes the five Ages of Man.

events.title: Thales predicts a solar eclipse
events.descr: According to Herodotus. Thales (c. 626/623 – c. 548/545 BC) was one of the Seven Sages.

events.title: Pythagoras founds a school at Croton
events.descr: The philosopher and polymath (c. 570 – c. 495 BC), eponymous founder of Pythagoreanism, travels to Croton in southern Italy.

events.title: Battle of Thermopylae
events.descr: Greek city-states led by Sparta under Leonidas I hold off Xerxes’ invasion force before the Persians win; the Greeks defeat the invaders at Salamis later that year.

events.title: Pericles leads Athens
events.descr: The statesman and general of the Golden Age of Athens dies of the Plague of Athens in 429 BC.

events.title: The Parthenon built
events.descr: A temple on the Athenian Acropolis dedicated to Athena, begun when the Delian League was at the peak of its power; work on its decoration continued until 432 BC.

events.title: The trial and death of Socrates
events.descr: Athens tries the 70-year-old philosopher on two charges and he is put to death.

events.title: Plato founds the Academy
events.descr: Aristotle studies there for twenty years (367–347 BC); the school lasts until 83 BC.

events.title: Aristotle founds the Lyceum
events.descr: Returning to Athens after it fell under Macedonian rule, Aristotle sets up his school at the Lyceum.

events.title: The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus
events.descr: The tomb of Mausolus, built between 353 and 351 BC in Halicarnassus; one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

events.title: Herodotus, historian of the Greco-Persian Wars
events.descr: A Greek historian and geographer from Halicarnassus; nothing in his Histories can be dated with certainty after 430 BC.

events.title: Life of Confucius
events.descr: Traditionally the paragon of Chinese sages; his teachings, Confucianism, emphasise personal and governmental morality.

events.title: Laozi (traditional dates)
events.descr: Considered the author of the Tao Te Ching and the founder of Taoism. Tradition makes him a contemporary of Confucius; he is sometimes dated to the 4th century BC, and the oldest manuscript of his book dates to the late 4th century BC.

events.title: Sun Tzu (traditional dates)
events.descr: The general and strategist traditionally credited with The Art of War, though its earliest parts probably date at least a century after him.

events.title: Mozi founds Mohism
events.descr: A philosophy emphasising universal love, social order, the will of Heaven, sharing and honouring the worthy.

events.title: The Hundred Schools of Thought
events.descr: Confucianism, Taoism, Mohism, Legalism and others flourish in the late Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods; their ideas profoundly influence East Asian culture.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Confucianism, Taoism, Mohism and Legalism
lead, Confucianism, Taoism, Mohism and Legalism

events.title: Shang Yang’s reforms in Qin
events.descr: The reformer takes office in Qin in 359 BCE; his first reforms (356 BC) assign land by military merit and favour agriculture, and a second set follows in 350 BC.

events.title: Pāṇini’s Sanskrit grammar
events.descr: The ancient Sanskrit grammarian flourished in the mid 1st millennium BCE, variously dated between the 6th–5th and the 4th century BCE.

events.title: Tiglath-Pileser I fights the Arameans
events.descr: The first certain reference to the Arameans: an inscription of Tiglath-Pileser I calls them the "Ahlamu of the land Armaya". He campaigns in the Levant against the Arameans and other tribal peoples; late in his reign Aramaean tribesmen put pressure on his realm.

events.title: Suteans and Arameans enter Babylonia
events.descr: West Semitic-speaking tribes arrive from the Levant: the earliest waves are Suteans and Arameans, followed a century or so later by the Kaldu (Chaldeans).

source.sourceLocation: Ancient Chaldeans ('appeared in Babylonia, c. 1100 BC')

events.title: Assyria withdraws; Aramean states take the west
events.descr: The Middle Assyrian Empire shrinks rapidly after Ashur-bel-kala, its last great ruler, dies in 1056 BC. The Arameans gain independence and take firm control of Eber-Nari, and in the 11th and 10th centuries conquer Sam'al (renamed Bît-Agushi) and Til Barsip, chief town of Bît-Adini.

source.sourceLocation: Aramean states ('in the late 11th century BC')

events.title: Ashur-dan II retakes land from the Arameans
events.descr: The first Assyrian king to campaign regularly in over a century; his annals present the wars against the Aramaeans to the west as retaking Assyrian territory. His successor Adad-nirari II (911–891 BC) marches as far as the Balikh river and the middle Euphrates.

events.title: Battle of Qarqar
events.descr: A coalition led by Aram-Damascus and Israel meets Shalmaneser III of Assyria. The Qedarite Gindibuʾ brings 1000 camelry, and Aḫuni of Bit-Adini joins the Levantine states.

events.title: Shalmaneser III annexes Bit-Adini
events.descr: The Aramean kingdom with its capital at Til Barsib is conquered and absorbed into the Assyrian Empire. (The page also places Aḫuni in the 853 Qarqar coalition, after this date.)

events.title: Aramaic becomes the lingua franca of the Assyrian empire
events.descr: Imperial Aramaic becomes the empire's common language under Tiglath-Pileser III; it stays a lingua franca under the Neo-Babylonian and Achaemenid empires.

events.title: Chaldeans first recorded
events.descr: Shalmaneser III subjugates Mushallim-Marduk, chief of the Amukani tribe: the first written attestation of the Chaldeans. Their tribes include Bit-Yâkin, Bet-Dakuri, Bet-Adini, Bet-Amukkani and Bet-Shilani.

events.title: A Chaldean takes the Babylonian throne
events.descr: The Chaldeans come to historical prominence in Babylonia for the first time when Marduk-apla-usur usurps the throne.

events.title: Marduk-apla-iddina II holds Babylon against Assyria
events.descr: A Chaldean of the Bit-Yakin tribe seizes the Babylonian throne from Assyrian control. An Assyrian attempt to defeat him near Der in 720 fails, but Sargon II eventually drives him from Babylon.

events.title: Marduk-apla-iddina II's second reign
events.descr: He reigns nine months before Sennacherib defeats him near Kish; he flees to Elam and dies in exile. The Qedarites back his revolt (his supporter Bašqanu is the brother of an Arab queen named Yaṯiʿe).

events.title: Naram-Sin defeats Sumerians and Amorites at Jebel Bishri
events.descr: A royal inscription records Naram-Sin of Akkad defeating a coalition of Sumerian cities and Amorites near Jebel Bishri.

events.title: Victory Stele of Naram-Sin over the Lullubi
events.descr: The stele shows Naram-Sin's victory over the Lullubi mountain tribe and their king Satuni; his inscription names Sidur and Sutuni, princes of the Lulubi, who "made war against me".

sources.sourceLocation: Akkadian Empire and Gutian dynasty (stele caption)
Akkadian Empire and Gutian dynasty (stele caption)

events.title: Tupkish, king of Urkesh and Nagar
events.descr: The first known Hurrian kingdom centres on Urkesh (Tell Mozan). Tupkish, a king with a Hurrian name, rules during the ascendancy of Akkad; seals of Tar'am-Agade, a daughter of Naram-Sin, were found at the site.

events.title: Hurrians spread into northern Syria
events.descr: By 1725 BC Hurrians are found in parts of northern Syria such as Alalakh; those entering at the end of the 17th century BC bring important political and cultural changes. The Hurrian entity of Mitanni first rises to power before 1550 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: Middle Bronze Age and Late Bronze Age
Middle Bronze Age and Late Bronze Age

events.title: Urkesh abandoned
events.descr: The city appears to have been largely abandoned around 1350 BCE, for reasons unknown.

events.title: Assyria conquers Shupria
events.descr: Shupria stays an independent kingdom after the destruction of Mitanni until Assyria conquers it. By the Early Iron Age the Hurrians had been assimilated with other peoples.

events.title: The Kaska first appear in Hittite prayers
events.descr: They appear in prayers from the reign of Hantili II; Tudhaliya II's third campaign is against the Kaskas, and Arnuwanda I prays for the return of Nerik and tries to buy off some Kaska with tribute.

events.title: Kaska burn Hattusa; the court moves to Samuha
events.descr: Sometime between Arnuwanda I and Suppiluliuma I, the Kaska join Hayasa-Azzi and Isuwa to burn Hattusa to the ground. Tudhaliya III and Suppiluliuma I hold court at Samuha; Suppiluliuma defeats Piyapili's united tribes and Hattusa returns to the Hittites. The Kaska could field as many as 9,000 warriors and 800 chariots.

source.sourceLocation: History (Tudhaliya III and Suppiluliuma I at Samuha, 'c. 1375–1350 BC')

events.title: Kaska sack Hattusa again
events.descr: In the early 13th century, while Muwatalli II is king, the Kaskas sack Hattusa; Hattusili III later recaptures Nerik.

events.title: Mushki and Kaska attack Alzi; Ashur-Dan I drives them back
events.descr: The Eastern Mushki, who moved into Hatti around the time the Hittite Empire collapsed, join the Urumu and the Kaska (Apishlu) in an attempt on Alzi and Puruhuzzi; Ashur-Dan I pushes them back and subjugates them.

events.title: Tiglath-Pileser I turns back the Mushki
events.descr: The Mushki push into Kadmuhi on the upper Tigris and are turned away by Tiglath-Pileser I, apparently settling in Alzi. He also records the Kaska ("Apishlu") late in the 12th century, after which they disappear from the records.

source.sourceLocation: Reign ('first campaign was against the Phrygians (Mushku) in 1112 BC')

events.title: Mita of the Mushki becomes Sargon II's ally
events.descr: After joining an anti-Assyrian alliance with Tabal and Carchemish, the Mushki under Mita re-emerge as allies of Assyria; Sargon names Mita his friend. Assyrian sources identify the Western Mushki with the Phrygians, and some scholars think Mita became King Midas.

events.title: Queen Zabibe pays tribute to Tiglath-Pileser III
events.descr: With Rezin of Damascus, Menahem of Israel and Hiram II of Tyre, she acknowledges Assyrian hegemony: the first explicit mention of the Qedarites by name.

events.title: Queen Šamši rebels; Assyria wins at Mount Saqurri
events.descr: Šamši pledges allegiance after the 734 campaign and rebels in 733. Tiglath-Pileser III defeats the Qedarites near Mount Saqurri; she flees to the Wadi Sirhan but keeps her throne and later pays 125 white camels.

events.title: Sennacherib campaigns against the Qedarites
events.descr: Queen Teʾelḫunu and her daughter Tabūʿa are captured at Dūmat, and Ḫazaʾil surrenders and pays tribute.

events.title: Qedarites join Šamaš-šuma-ukin's revolt
events.descr: King Abyaṯiʿ supports the revolt against Ashurbanipal, and the Qedarites are trapped in Babylon. After it is suppressed they raid Assyria's western borderlands with the Nabataeans.

events.title: King Mu of Zhou defeats the Quanrong
events.descr: The following year he attacks the Western Rong and the Xurong.

events.title: Western Rong and Xianyun raid deep into Zhou
events.descr: Under King Li. His successor King Xuan (827–782 BCE) sends Qin against the Western Rong, who submit and cede territory, and Jin against the Northern Rong.

events.title: The Quanrong sack Haojing and kill King You
events.descr: The Marquess of Shen invites the Quanrong to join an attack on King You; the joint force occupies the capital Haojing, kills him and captures Bao Si. (The Xinian bamboo slips say King You attacked Shen, who allied with the Quanrong.) This ends the Western Zhou.

events.title: The Red Di take the capital of Wey
events.descr: They kill its ruler but are driven out by Qi. Jin fights many wars with the Di from 660 to 507 BC. The page marks these entries as needing citations.

events.title: The Rong fade from the record
events.descr: After 650 BCE the Rong are rarely mentioned; they seem to have been mostly absorbed by the states of Qi and Jin.

events.title: Zhongshan, a non-Zhou state in the north
events.descr: Some sources (Records of the Grand Historian) say Beidi founded and ruled it; others list it only as not Zhou or Han. Wei conquers it in 407, it regains independence in 381, and Zhao annexes it after ten years of war.

source.sourceLocation: History ('in 414 BC ... traditionally considered the founding')

events.title: Qin defeats the last hostile Rong tribe
events.descr: By 400 BC most of the Di and Rong had been eliminated as independent polities.

events.title: The Medjay first recorded
events.descr: The Autobiography of Weni, from the reign of Pepi I, is the first written mention of the Medjay. Until the end of the Second Intermediate Period the word denotes a Nubian people.

events.title: Medjay: from desert people to Egyptian police
events.descr: The page dates the pan-graves to the late Middle Kingdom and Second Intermediate Period. Medjay serve in Kamose's campaign against the Hyksos; by the 18th Dynasty they are an elite paramilitary police force, and after the 20th Dynasty the term no longer appears in Egyptian records.

sources.sourceLocation: Origins, Pan-graves, Police force and Demise
Origins, Pan-graves, Police force and Demise

events.title: "Land of the Shasu yhw" in Egyptian texts
events.descr: A list of Egypt's enemies on column bases at Amenhotep III's temple at Soleb includes the name; Egyptian texts refer to 'the Land of the Shasu yhwꜣ'; a 13th-century copy at Amara, under Seti I or Ramesses II, names six Shasu groups. Astour notes this predates the Mesha Stele's use of the divine name by over 500 years. Shasu raids could cut Egypt's northern routes, prompting punitive campaigns by Ramesses II and Merneptah.

sources.sourceLocation: History, Late Bronze Age and Shasu of Yhw

source.sourceLocation: Shasu of Yhw ('the period of Amenhotep III (14th century BCE)')

sources.sourceLocation: History, Late Bronze Age and Shasu of Yhw

events.title: Death of Alexander the Great
events.descr: He dies at the age of 32, between the evenings of 10 and 11 June 323 BCE; fighting between his generals starts almost immediately.

events.title: Wars of the Diadochi
events.descr: Conflicts between Alexander’s generals over his empire. Ptolemy receives Egypt; after Corupedium (281 BC) Seleucus I is the last of the original successors, and Macedon is settled for the Antigonids only in 272 BC with the death of Pyrrhus.

events.title: Battle of Ipsus
events.descr: A coalition of Seleucus, Cassander and Lysimachus defeats Antigonus I, who is killed.

events.title: Seleucus takes Babylon: the Seleucid Empire
events.descr: After the battle of Gaza (312 BC), Seleucus captures the citadel of Babylon in August 311 BC. His empire is annexed by Rome under Pompey in 63 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox, Rise of Seleucus and Babylonian War
lead, infobox, Rise of Seleucus and Babylonian War

events.title: Ptolemy I becomes pharaoh: the Ptolemaic Kingdom
events.descr: Ptolemy, who had ruled Egypt as satrap since 323 BC, takes the title of basileus and pharaoh. The kingdom lasts until the death of Cleopatra VII in 30 BC.

events.title: The Library of Alexandria
events.descr: Probably built under Ptolemy II Philadelphus (285–246 BC), though Ptolemy I may have planned it. Its decline begins with a purge of intellectuals in 145 BC; part is burned by Julius Caesar in 48 BC.

events.title: The Greco-Bactrian Kingdom breaks away
events.descr: Founded by the Seleucid satrap Diodotus I; it falls around 120 BC as the Parthians and nomads such as the Saka and Yuezhi press in. The Yuezhi later found the Kushan Empire.

events.title: Archimedes killed at the siege of Syracuse
events.descr: One of the greatest mathematicians of all time (c. 287 – c. 212 BC), he designed war machines to defend Syracuse and was killed by a Roman soldier.

events.title: The Rosetta Stone decree
events.descr: A decree issued at Memphis on behalf of Ptolemy V Epiphanes on 27 March 196 BC.

events.title: Battle of Pydna: Rome ends the Antigonid kingdom
events.descr: Defeat in the Third Macedonian War ends the dynasty that had ruled much of Hellenistic Greece since 294 BC.

events.title: Attalus III leaves Pergamon to Rome
events.descr: The childless king bequeaths his realm to the Roman Republic; after a revolt it becomes the Roman province of Asia (129 BC).

events.title: First Punic War
events.descr: It breaks out on Sicily and lasts twenty-three years, until Carthage is defeated.

events.title: Second Punic War: Hannibal
events.descr: Hannibal is defeated at Zama in 202 BC and a treaty follows in 201 BC.

events.title: Rome destroys Carthage
events.descr: Rome declares war in 149 BC and storms Carthage in 146 BC; its territory becomes the Roman province of Africa.

events.title: Battle of Carrhae: Parthia defeats Crassus
events.descr: Fought between the Roman Republic and the Parthian Empire; Cicero called the war "nulla causa", since Parthia had a treaty with Rome.

events.title: Julius Caesar assassinated
events.descr: Killed on the Ides of March (15 March), three days before he was to leave on a campaign against the Parthians; the Liberators’ civil war follows (43–42 BC).

events.title: Battle of Actium
events.descr: On 2 September 31 BC Octavian’s fleet under Agrippa defeats Antony and Cleopatra. Cleopatra takes her life on 12 August 30 BC, ending the Ptolemaic Kingdom and the Hellenistic period, and Egypt becomes a Roman province.

events.title: Octavian becomes Augustus: the Roman Empire
events.descr: The Senate grants Octavian the title Augustus on 16 January 27 BC, often seen as the end of the Republic. He rules as the first emperor until his death in AD 14 and makes peace with Parthia and Kush.

events.title: The Roman Empire at its greatest extent
events.descr: At the time of Trajan’s death (r. 98–117 AD) the empire covers some 5,000,000 km².

events.title: Crisis of the Third Century
events.descr: It begins with the assassination of Severus Alexander by his own troops; by 268 the empire has split into three competing states, and Aurelian (270–275) turns the tide.

events.title: The Tetrarchy
events.descr: Diocletian divides imperial rule between two augusti and two caesares; the system lasts until c. 324.

events.title: Edict of Milan
events.descr: The 13 February 313 agreement to treat Christians benevolently; Christianity becomes the state religion with the Edict of Thessalonica in 380.

events.title: Constantinople becomes the capital
events.descr: Founded in 324 on the site of Byzantium and dedicated on 11 May 330 as the capital of the Roman Empire.

events.title: Battle of Adrianople
events.descr: In 376 the Huns had driven many Goths into the empire; at Adrianople the Goths under Fritigern defeat the emperor Valens, who is killed in battle.

events.title: Death of Theodosius I: East and West divide
events.descr: He dies after making Christianity the state religion, ending the unified empire (27 BC – AD 395).

sources.sourceLocation: infobox and Transition to late antiquity
infobox and Transition to late antiquity

events.title: The Visigoths sack Rome
events.descr: On 24 August 410 Alaric’s Visigoths enter Rome and pillage it for three days. The Vandals sack it again in 455.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Third siege and sack, and Aftermath
infobox, lead, Third siege and sack, and Aftermath
infobox, lead, Third siege and sack, and Aftermath

events.title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
events.descr: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus, the last Western emperor, and sends the imperial insignia to the Eastern emperor Zeno.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and Fall in the West

events.title: Reign of Justinian I
events.descr: He rewrites Roman law as the Corpus Juris Civilis (final code 534) and retakes North Africa from the Vandals (533–534) and Italy from the Ostrogoths; the empire reaches its territorial zenith in 555.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, Life, Legislative activities, Conquest of North Africa, War in Italy and Results
infobox, Life, Legislative activities, Conquest of North Africa, War in Italy and Results

events.title: Hagia Sophia built
events.descr: Justinian’s basilica rises after the second church burns in the Nika riots of January 532; it is inaugurated on 27 December 537.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox and Church of Justinian I
lead, infobox and Church of Justinian I

events.title: The Plague of Justinian
events.descr: It reaches Roman Egypt in 541 and every corner of the empire by 543; Justinian catches it and recovers. It strikes the Sasanian Empire too and recurs until the mid-8th century.

events.title: The Parthian Empire
events.descr: Centred in ancient Iran; Mithridates I (r. c. 171–132 BC) greatly expands it by seizing Media and Mesopotamia from the Seleucids.

events.title: The Maccabean Revolt
events.descr: A revolt against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV’s repression of Judaism. The Maccabees take Jerusalem in 164 BCE; Judas Maccabeus dies in 160, and in 141 Simon Thassi expels the Greeks. An alliance with Rome helps secure independence.

events.title: Herod the Great rules Judea
events.descr: A Roman client king; after his death the Romans divide his kingdom among three of his sons and his sister. Some scholars (Steinmann) date his reign 36–1 BCE.

events.title: Crucifixion of Jesus
events.descr: In Jerusalem, in the Roman province of Judaea; dated AD 30 or 33.

events.title: Rome destroys Jerusalem and the Second Temple
events.descr: The decisive event of the First Jewish Revolt (66–73 CE): the siege runs from 13 April to 8 September 70.

events.title: The Bar Kokhba revolt
events.descr: Its primary cause is generally held to be Hadrian’s plan to rebuild Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina; the rebels hold an independent state for over three years until Betar falls in 135. The province is renamed Syria Palaestina.

events.title: Rome annexes the Nabataean Kingdom
events.descr: Independent since the mid-3rd century BC, it becomes the province of Arabia Petraea.

events.title: The Sasanian Empire
events.descr: Ardashir I defeats the Parthians at the Battle of Hormozdgan on 28 April 224; the last pre-Islamic Iranian empire rules until 651.

events.title: Shapur I defeats Rome at Edessa
events.descr: A tremendous defeat for the Romans: in 260, probably in June, the emperor Valerian is defeated at Edessa and held prisoner by Shapur I; the date of his death in captivity is debated. The same year Odaenathus of Palmyra defeats Shapur near the Euphrates.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox, Rule and fall, Death in captivity

events.title: Zenobia’s Palmyrene Empire
events.descr: In 270 Zenobia rapidly conquers most of the Roman east, including Egypt; in 271 she claims the imperial title. Aurelian besieges Palmyra in 272 and razes it after a revolt in 273.

events.title: Armenia adopts Christianity
events.descr: The traditional date; scholars propose dates from 284 to no later than 325, and many favour 314.

events.title: Aksum conquers Himyar
events.descr: After the conquest Christianity becomes Himyar’s main religion; Sasanian intervention brings Yemen under Persian influence in 575 or 578.

events.title: The last Roman–Persian war
events.descr: The Sasanians conquer much of the Levant, parts of Anatolia and, for the first time, Egypt; they take Jerusalem after a three-week siege in 614. Heraclius strikes back from 622, the Persians fail before Constantinople in 626, and Persia, torn by civil war, seeks peace.

events.title: The Hijrah: start of the Islamic calendar
events.descr: Its date equates to 16 July 622; the year is the epoch of the Islamic calendar.

events.title: Battle of the Yarmuk
events.descr: On 15–20 August 636 the Rashidun Caliphate defeats the Byzantine army; Byzantine Syria is annexed.

events.title: Battle of al-Qadisiyyah
events.descr: The second Rashidun invasion of Sasanian territory wins a decisive victory (16–19 November 636).

events.title: Fall of the Sasanian Empire
events.descr: By 651 most cities of the Iranian lands are in Muslim hands; the Rashidun Caliphate annexes the empire.

events.title: Chandragupta Maurya founds the Maurya Empire
events.descr: His conquest of Magadha is generally dated to c. 322–319 BCE; an alternative chronology places these events in c. 311–305 BCE. He reigns until c. 297 BCE.

events.title: Seleucid–Mauryan war
events.descr: Fought sometime between 305 and 303 BCE between Chandragupta and Seleucus I Nicator; it ends in a marriage alliance.

events.title: Reign of Ashoka
events.descr: Mauryan emperor from c. 268 BCE until his death in 232 BCE. His reputation grows after the 19th-century decipherment of sources written in the Brahmi script.

events.title: Kalinga War
events.descr: Ashoka conquers Kalinga in the eighth year of his reign, according to his own edicts. The war began an era of more than 40 years of relative peace.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, Course of the war and Aftermath

source.sourceLocation: infobox and Course of the war

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, Course of the war and Aftermath

events.title: Buddhism reaches Sri Lanka
events.descr: Theravada Buddhism is introduced during the reign of King Devanampiya Tissa.

events.title: Pushyamitra Shunga kills the last Maurya
events.descr: The assassination of Brihadratha by Pushyamitra Shunga ends the Maurya Empire and begins the Shunga Empire.

events.title: Demetrius I invades India: the Indo-Greek Kingdom
events.descr: The Graeco-Bactrian king Demetrius I invades India from Bactria. The Indo-Greeks disappear as a political entity around 10 AD.

events.title: Menander I
events.descr: Indo-Greek king; the precise dates of his reign remain elusive. Patanjali’s Mahabhashya, around 150 BC, describes a failed campaign of Menander as far as Mathura. According to tradition, he embraced the Buddhist faith.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Reign and Menander and Buddhism
infobox, lead, Reign and Menander and Buddhism

events.title: Maues, the first Saka king in India
events.descr: The first rulers of the Indo-Scythian kingdom are Maues (c. 85–60 BCE) and Vonones (c. 75–65 BCE).

events.title: Kujula Kadphises unites the Yuezhi: the Kushan Empire
events.descr: Kujula Kadphises (25–85), the first ruler, unites the Yuezhi tribes into a confederation. The Kushan Empire fragments into semi-independent kingdoms in the 3rd century AD.

events.title: A Kushan army fights Ban Chao near Khotan
events.descr: Ban Chao fights battles near Khotan with a Kushan army of 70,000 men.

sources.sourceLocation: Conquests in India and Central Asia
Conquests in India and Central Asia

events.title: Reign of Kanishka
events.descr: The empire reaches its zenith. Around 127 CE he replaces Greek with Bactrian as the official language of administration. He never converts to Buddhism but gives it royal sponsorship, and heads the 4th Buddhist Council in Kashmir. Earlier scholars dated his accession to 78 CE.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox and Kanishka and Buddhism
lead, infobox and Kanishka and Buddhism

events.title: Naneghat inscription of Satakarni I
events.descr: Dated to 70–60 BCE, in the reign of Satakarni I.

events.title: The Pallavas become a major southern power
events.descr: During the reigns of Mahendravarman I (600–630) and Narasimhavarman I (630–668).

events.title: Kashyapa I rules from Sigiriya
events.descr: Kashyapa I (473–491) chooses Sigiriya to be his capital.

events.title: Coronation of Chandragupta I
events.descr: Crowned on 26 February 320. The Gupta Empire, established c. 240, exists from the mid 3rd century to the mid 6th century CE.

events.title: Reign of Samudragupta
events.descr: The second Gupta emperor. Modern scholars variously assign the start of his reign from c. 319 CE to c. 350 CE.

events.title: Reign of Chandragupta II
events.descr: Gupta emperor until his death in c. 415. The beginning of his reign can be dated to either 376–377 CE or 380–381 CE.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox and Period of reign
lead, infobox and Period of reign

events.title: Chandragupta II defeats the last Western Satrap
events.descr: Rudrasimha III, the last of the Western Satraps, is defeated by the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II.

events.title: Nalanda founded
events.descr: Established by the Gupta emperor Kumaragupta I; it operates for almost a thousand years, until around 1400 CE.

events.title: Gupta–Hunnic Wars
events.descr: Wars between the Gupta Empire and the Huns; the Alchon Huns invade India between the 4th and 6th centuries CE.

events.title: Ajanta Caves: the second phase
events.descr: Buddhist cave monuments dating from the second century BCE to about 480 CE. The second phase falls in a brief period of 460–480 CE according to later scholarship (400–650 CE in older accounts), circa 480 CE under King Harishena.

events.title: Aryabhata
events.descr: Mathematician-astronomer of the Gupta era. He states he was 23 years old in 3600 Kali Yuga, 499 CE. His Aryabhatiya is translated into Arabic c. 820 CE.

events.title: Harsha, emperor of Kannauj
events.descr: Crowned at an assembly in April 606, after the downfall of the Gupta Empire in the middle of the 6th century; he rules until his death in 647. An invasion he leads is repelled on the banks of the Narmada in the winter of 618–619.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox, Early years and Reign
lead, infobox, Early years and Reign

events.title: Tang Taizong sends Wang Xuance to India
events.descr: The Tang Chinese emperor Tang Taizong sends Wang Xuance to India.

events.title: Qin unifies China
events.descr: Beginning in 230 BC, the Qin under King Ying Zheng wage a series of wars; by 221 BC he has conquered all the other warring states, ending the Warring States period, and rules as Qin Shi Huang.

events.title: Qin Shi Huang dies; the Terracotta Army
events.descr: Qin Shi Huang dies on 12 July 210 BC, during his fifth tour of eastern China. Work on his mausoleum began in 246 BCE; the Terracotta Army was buried with him in 210–209 BCE and discovered by farmers on 29 March 1974.

events.title: Liu Bang proclaimed emperor: the Han dynasty
events.descr: The Qin surrender to Liu Bang in 207 BC and Xianyang is destroyed in 206 BC. After the Battle of Gaixia (202 BC), Liu Bang is proclaimed emperor (Emperor Gaozu, 202–195 BC). Western Han: 202 BC – 9 AD; Eastern Han: 25–220 AD.

events.title: Reign of Emperor Wu of Han
events.descr: The seventh emperor of the Han dynasty, from 141 until his death in 87 BC; his reign lasts 54 years. In 104 BC a new calendar is put into effect.

events.title: Zhang Qian sent to the Western Regions
events.descr: Emperor Wu dispatches his envoy Zhang Qian into the Western Regions.

events.title: Sima Qian’s Shiji
events.descr: Sima Qian (c. 145 – c. 86 BC), historian of the early Han, completes it before 91 BC, probably around 94 BC. In 99 BC he becomes embroiled in the Li Ling affair; released from prison in 96 BC, he lives on as a palace eunuch.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and As Han court official

source.sourceLocation: As Han court official (probably around 94 BC)

sources.sourceLocation: lead and As Han court official

events.title: The Xin dynasty interrupts the Han
events.descr: Between the Western Han (202 BC – 9 AD) and the Eastern Han (25–220 AD).

events.title: Cai Lun improves papermaking
events.descr: A eunuch official at the court in Luoyang, he substantially improves the papermaking process; earlier forms of paper have existed since the 3rd century BCE.

events.title: Yellow Turban Rebellion
