events.descr: It breaks out in March 184, during the reign of Emperor Ling. The main rebellion is suppressed by 185, but subduing the resisting areas takes until 205.

events.title: Battle of Red Cliffs
events.descr: A battle on the Yangtze River in the winter of 208–209. Cao Cao’s southern campaign had started in the autumn of 208.

events.title: End of the Han: the Three Kingdoms
events.descr: The Han abdicates to Cao Wei. The Three Kingdoms period runs from the establishment of Cao Wei in 220 to the conquest of Wu by Jin in 280; other starts proposed include 184, 189, 190 and 196.

events.title: Jin reunites China
events.descr: The Western Jin, established in 266 as successor to Cao Wei, conquers Eastern Wu, ending the Three Kingdoms period. Shu Han had fallen to Wei in 263.

events.title: War of the Eight Princes
events.descr: A series of civil wars; in 304 the dynasty faces a wave of rebellions, the start of the Sixteen Kingdoms.

events.title: Luoyang sacked; the Jin move south
events.descr: Luoyang is sacked in 311 and Chang’an captured in 316, ending the Western Jin (266–316). In 317 the Eastern Jin begins at Jiankang, south of the Huai River.

events.title: The Eastern Jin defeat the Former Qin
events.descr: A devastating defeat for the Former Qin, which from 376 to 383 had unified all of northern and northwest China and Sichuan.

events.title: Northern Wei unifies the north
events.descr: The unification of northern China ends the Sixteen Kingdoms period. The Northern Wei, established on 20 February 386, rules from Pingcheng from 398 until it moves its capital to Luoyang on 25 October 493.

events.title: Sui reunites China
events.descr: Yang Jian takes the throne on 4 March 581; in 588 the Sui mass 518,000 troops along the Yangtze, and by 589 Sui troops enter Jiankang.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox and Foundation and Emperor Wen
infobox and Foundation and Emperor Wen

events.title: The Grand Canal completed
events.descr: The network is expanded and completed by Emperor Yang of Sui; its oldest sections date to the early 5th century BC.

events.title: The Tang dynasty founded
events.descr: Established on 18 June 618; the Sui is abolished by Li Yuan (Emperor Gaozu of Tang, 618–626). Emperor Yang of Sui had been assassinated by Yuwen Huaji in 618.

events.title: Xuanwu Gate Incident
events.descr: A palace coup for the Tang throne on 2 July 626. Within three days Li Shimin is crown prince; about two months later Emperor Gaozu abdicates in his favour (Emperor Taizong, 626–649).

events.title: Wiman seizes Gojoseon
events.descr: The ruling dynasty of Old Chosŏn is overthrown by Wiman. Tradition places the founding by Tan’gun in 2333 BCE, a date the page calls mythological.

events.title: Han conquers Gojoseon
events.descr: The Han dynasty under Emperor Wu invades and conquers Wiman Joseon in the Gojoseon–Han War and establishes commanderies in its place (Lelang, 108 BCE – 313 CE; Xuantu from 107 BCE).

events.title: Goguryeo annexes Lelang
events.descr: Lelang had been ruled by the Jin dynasty until 313. Daifang falls in 314–315 and Xuantu in 319.

events.title: Goguryeo adopts Buddhism
events.descr: The first of the Korean kingdoms to do so; Baekje accepts Buddhism in 384, and Silla adopts it in 527–528.

events.title: Campaigns of Gwanggaeto the Great
events.descr: Goguryeo’s capital moves from Gungnae to Pyongyang in 427.

events.title: Baekje loses the Seoul region
events.descr: The Seoul region falls to Goguryeo; Baekje’s capital is at Ungjin (Gongju) from 475 to 538, when King Seong moves it to Sabi.

events.title: Silla adopts Buddhism
events.descr: Buddhism becomes Silla’s state and official religion from 527.

events.title: Goguryeo–Sui War
events.descr: Sui’s campaigns end in defeat by 614.

events.title: Goguryeo–Tang War
events.descr: Silla, allied with Tang China, conquers Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668 (the fall of Pyongyang).

events.title: The Yamato kingship begins
events.descr: Usually believed to have begun c. 250. Kofun tombs are built for the ruling class from the 3rd to the 7th centuries.

events.title: Buddhism reaches Japan
events.descr: According to the Nihon Shoki (720), Buddhism and the Chinese characters are introduced from Baekje; the date marks the end of the Kofun period and the start of the Asuka period.

events.title: Seventeen-article constitution
events.descr: According to the Nihon Shoki of 720, a document authored by Prince Shōtoku, adopted in the reign of Empress Suiko (r. 593–628).

events.title: Isshi incident and the Taika Reform
events.descr: A palace coup on 10 July 645 (the Isshi incident) is followed by the Taika Reform; the era of 645–649 is named Taika.

events.title: Modu Chanyu founds the Xiongnu Empire
events.descr: Modu kills his father Touman in 209 BCE and rules until 174 BCE. By 208 BCE the Donghu are defeated (they splinter into the Xianbei and Wuhuan), and in 203 BCE he defeats the Yuezhi.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead and Rise of the Xiongnu Empire
infobox, lead and Rise of the Xiongnu Empire

events.title: Battle of Baideng
events.descr: A Han dynasty vanguard, in an army led by Emperor Gaozu, is encircled at Mount Baideng near Pingcheng for seven days. In 198 BC a marriage alliance (heqin) is concluded between the Han and the Xiongnu.

events.title: The Xiongnu defeat the Yuezhi
events.descr: After a major defeat, the Yuezhi split into two groups; the majority begin migrating west to the Ili valley in 165 BCE.

events.title: The Great Yuezhi settle in Bactria
events.descr: The Wusun drive the Great Yuezhi out of the Ili valley; they migrate west, then south, and settle in northern Bactria, where the Han envoy Zhang Qian reaches them in 128 BCE. Around 30 CE one of their tribes, the Kushana, forms the basis of the Kushan Empire.

sources.sourceLocation: timeline table and Exodus of the Great Yuezhi
lead and Migration to the Ili Valley
timeline table and Exodus of the Great Yuezhi

events.title: Han–Xiongnu wars
events.descr: The tension fully escalates in 133 BC; between 127 and 119 BC Han campaigns push into Mongolia, with a decisive campaign in 119 BC, and a regional protectorate is set up in 60 BC. Some date the conflicts as early as 200 BC and as late as 188 AD.

events.title: The Xiongnu split in two
events.descr: In 46 AD repeated natural disasters severely weaken the Xiongnu; they permanently split into two groups in 48 AD.

events.title: Defeat of the Northern Xiongnu
events.descr: In 89 AD Dou Xian leads 50,000 cavalry against them; in 91 AD the Northern Chanyu is defeated in the Battle of the Altai Mountains, and the Xianbei take over the Mongolian Plateau, absorbing 100,000 Xiongnu tribes.

events.title: Tanshihuai unifies the Xianbei
events.descr: He unifies the Xianbei in the mid-2nd century and raids the Han dynasty’s northern borders, with a first recorded raid in 156; after his death in 181 the Xianbei splinter.

events.title: Bumin overthrows the Rouran: the Turkic Khaganate
events.descr: In 552 Bumin defeats Anagui north of Huaihuang, effectively ending the Rouran, which had dominated the eastern steppe for a century and a half; Muqan Qaghan finishes off the remaining Rouran, who resist until 555.

events.title: Turkic and Byzantine embassies
events.descr: First contact is believed to have happened in 563; a Turkic embassy arrives in 568, and in 569 an embassy led by Zemarchus follows.

sources.sourceLocation: History > Relations with the Byzantine Empire
History > Relations with the Byzantine Empire

events.title: The Turkic Khaganate splits
events.descr: A civil war follows Taspar Qaghan’s death in 581, the year the Sui dynasty is founded. Tardu briefly reunifies the empire (599–603); after him it splits again in 603 into Eastern and Western khaganates.

events.title: Tang conquers the Eastern Turks
events.descr: Illig Qaghan, the last independent ruler, who had reached the gates of Chang’an in 626, is captured. Tang conquers the Western Turkic Khaganate in 657.

events.title: Kidarite kingdom in Bactria
events.descr: A Kidarite kingdom replaces the Kushano-Sasanians in Bactria; by 365 Kidara I puts his name on the coinage as Kushanshah. Circa 390–410 the Kidarites invade north-western India.

events.title: The Hephthalites defeat the Kidarites
events.descr: From 450 the Hephthalites are militarily important; by 479 they have conquered Sogdia and driven the Kidarites eastwards, and by 493 they hold parts of Dzungaria and the Tarim Basin.

events.title: Turks and Sasanians destroy the Hephthalites
events.descr: In 557 Istämi allies with Khosrow I of the Sasanian Empire; their combined forces defeat the Hephthalites in 560, who then survive as principalities in Tokharistan until 710.

events.title: The Alans appear in the Caucasus
events.descr: Between 50 and 60 CE the Alans appear in the foothills of the Caucasus. In the 3rd century the Goths break Sarmatian dominance of the Pontic Steppe.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and In the Pontic Steppe and Europe
lead and In the Pontic Steppe and Europe

events.title: The Huns reach the Volga
events.descr: By 370 the Huns have arrived on the Volga, causing the westward movement of Goths and Alans; in 376 the Goths cross the Danube. By 430 the Huns have a vast but short-lived empire on the Danubian frontier.

events.title: Attila rules the Huns
events.descr: He rules jointly with his brother Bleda until Bleda’s death in 445; in 441 he invades the Eastern Roman Empire. He dies in early 453.

events.title: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
events.descr: On 20 June 451, after Attila crosses the Rhine and invades Gaul, Aetius and Theodoric (who is killed) meet him in battle; the result is inconclusive. In 452 the Huns invade Italy.

events.title: Battle of Nedao: the Hunnic empire breaks up
events.descr: After Attila’s death in 453 the Huns lose much of their empire. Attila’s son Dengizich dies in 469.

events.title: The Avar Khaganate
events.descr: The Pannonian Avars enter the historical scene in the mid-6th century; their khaganate is established in 567 and lasts until 822.

events.title: Avar–Byzantine wars
events.descr: The wars run from 568 to 626, the year the Avars are defeated by Samo.

events.title: Masinissa’s kingdom of Numidia
events.descr: During the Second Punic War Masinissa, king of the Massylii, defeats Syphax of the Masaesyli; with Scipio he beats Syphax and Hasdrubal at Cirta in 203 BC. After Zama (202 BC) he rules Numidia until his death in 148 BC, aged about 90, and by 158 BC has conquered Lepcis Magna and the Tripolitanian coast.

events.title: Masinissa’s war with Carthage
events.descr: Masinissa seizes more Carthaginian territory in 152 BC; in 151 BC he invades Carthaginian lands with 52,000 men. Carthage, by preparing to fight back, effectively breaks the peace treaty of 201 BC, and its general Hasdrubal is decisively defeated by Masinissa’s son Gulussa in 150 BC. In 146 BC Carthage is obliterated.

events.title: Jugurthine War
events.descr: In 113 BC Jugurtha again declares war on his cousin; Rome declares war on him in 111 BC, and Metellus arrives in Africa in 109 BC. Mauretania fights on Jugurtha’s side from 107 BC and on Rome’s in 105 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead and Jugurtha and Numidia
infobox, lead and Jugurtha and Numidia

events.title: Numidia becomes a Roman province
events.descr: Juba I’s reign (60–46 BC) ends. The Numidia infobox dates the annexation by the Roman Empire to 25 BC.

events.title: Juba II: Mauretania a Roman client kingdom
events.descr: After Bocchus II bequeaths his kingdom to Octavian (33 BC), Augustus makes Mauretania a client kingdom in 25 BC under Juba II, who marries Cleopatra Selene II the same year. In AD 21 Juba makes his son Ptolemy co-ruler.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox, History and monarch table
lead, infobox, History and monarch table

events.title: Rome annexes Mauretania
events.descr: Caligula orders the execution of King Ptolemy in 40 AD; after Aedemon’s death in 42 AD, Sabalus surrenders in 44 AD and the region is annexed to Rome.

events.title: Balbus campaigns against the Garamantes
events.descr: The Romans capture fifteen Garamantian settlements. The earliest known written record of the Garamantes dates to the 5th century BC; Herodotus includes them among the Libyan tribes.

events.title: Septimius Severus captures Garama
events.descr: The Garamantian capital falls to Rome. The Garamantes first emerge as a major regional power in the mid-2nd century AD and flourish until the late 7th century.

events.title: The Vandals cross into Africa
events.descr: An estimated 80,000 Vandals under Gaiseric cross from Hispania in 429. They besiege Hippo Regius in 430, where St. Augustine dies on 28 August 430, three months into the siege; peace is made with Rome in 435.

events.title: The Vandals take Carthage
events.descr: Gaiseric breaks the treaty and captures Carthage, which becomes his capital. The Vandals raid Sicily in 440, and peace is secured in 442.

events.title: The Vandals sack Rome
events.descr: The Vandal kingdom is primarily remembered for this sack of Rome in 455. In the 460s the Romans launch two expeditions by sea against it; both fail.

events.title: Belisarius conquers the Vandal kingdom
events.descr: The kingdom ends after 99 years; Gelimer (530–534) is its last ruler.

events.title: Royal burials move to Meroë: the Meroitic period
events.descr: Under Arakamani the royal burial ground moves from Napata to Meroë, and Napata loses its symbolic role. The pyramids of Meroë are built from c. 300 BC to about 350 AD.

events.title: The Meroitic script
events.descr: Developed at the beginning of the Meroitic period to write the Meroitic language; the cursive form predates the earliest surviving hieroglyphic inscription by a century or more. It was deciphered by Francis Llewellyn Griffith (1909, or 1911 in the body of the page).

source.sourceLocation: footnote 2 (Rilly: 'first half of the 3rd Cent. BC')

events.title: Kush at war with Rome; peace with Amanirenas
events.descr: After a Nubian attack on southern Egypt, the Roman governor Petronius invades Nubia and sacks Napata (22 BC; 23 BC on the Napata page). A peace treaty is signed in 22 BC between Rome and Meroë under Augustus and Amanirenas.

events.title: Nero’s expedition reaches Meroë
events.descr: In the autumn of 61 AD a Praetorian party sent by Nero reaches Meroë and goes up the White Nile to the Sudd. The kingdom begins to fade as a power by the 1st or 2nd century AD.

events.title: Aksum takes Meroë: the end of Kush
events.descr: Meroë is already in decline around 300. Aksumites capture Meroë and loot its gold, and Ezana takes the title “King of Ethiopia”; the Aksumite presence is short-lived, and Kush dissolves into Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia.

source.sourceLocation: Fourth Meroitic Period ('In 350 AD Meroë was destroyed by Axum')

events.title: Silko of Nobatia drives out the Blemmyes
events.descr: The first known king of Nobatia claims to have driven the Blemmyes into the Eastern Desert; the capital is set at Pachoras (Faras). The last known Meroitic inscription, of the Blemmye king Kharamadoye at Kalabsha, dates to AD 410/450.

events.title: Dongola founded
events.descr: The Makurian capital; a new Makurian state has emerged by the 5th century, after the collapse of Kush.

events.title: The temple at Philae is closed
events.descr: In the 530s the Byzantines under Justinian pursue a policy of expansion into Nubia.

events.title: The Nubian kingdoms convert to Christianity
events.descr: Nobatia converts in 543; Makuria has “received the faith of Christ” by around 568 and sends a delegation to Constantinople in 573. Alodia, first mentioned in 569, is the last: its request is granted in 580 and Longinus is sent.

events.title: Makuria annexes Nobatia
events.descr: Presumably during the 620s, but before 642; a new bishopric is founded in Faras around 630. The Nobatia page says only that the merger most likely came before 652, and certainly by 707.

events.title: Arab invasions of Makuria and the Baqt
events.descr: A first expedition comes in 641 or 642; a second, under Abd Allah ibn Sa’d ibn Abi al-Sarh, besieges Dongola in 651/652 and is repulsed. The resulting treaty with King Qalidurut, the Baqt, sends 360 slaves a year to Egypt and remains in force for more than six centuries. Alodia is explicitly not affected by it.

events.title: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
events.descr: A Greek merchants’ guide to the Red Sea and Indian Ocean; a mid-first-century date is now most commonly accepted. It describes the city of the Auxumites, its ivory trade, and its ruler Zoscales.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Date and authorship, and Aksum section
lead, Date and authorship, and Aksum section

events.title: Aksum begins minting coins
events.descr: Under King Endybis. Coins are known from eighteen Aksumite kings, from c. 295 until c. 620.

events.title: Reign of Ezana
events.descr: The first Aksumite king to embrace Christianity; his coins replace the pagan disc and crescent with a cross. A surviving letter from Constantius II is addressed to him and his brother Saizana.

events.title: Aksum becomes Christian
events.descr: Ezana converts; Frumentius, who came to Aksum as a child around 316, is consecrated its bishop. The coin weights suggest a conversion before Constantine’s reform of 324, or a few years after.

source.sourceLocation: Biography ('or according to others, between 340 and 346')

events.title: The stelae of Axum
events.descr: The Obelisk of Axum is probably carved and erected during the 4th century AD; the last stele raised in Axum is probably King Ezana’s Stele.

events.title: Reign of Kaleb; Aksum invades Yemen
events.descr: Kaleb invades Yemen around 520 (518–525 in the Aksum infobox), and Aksumite control of West Yemen lasts until c. 525, when Abraha deposes Sumyafa Ashwa. The envoy Nonnosus meets him in 530.

events.title: Aksumite–Persian wars
events.descr: The Aksum infobox lists the Year of the Elephant in 570 and the Aksumite–Persian wars from 570 to 578.

events.title: Muslims take refuge in Aksum
events.descr: The first Hijrah: a small group of early Muslims, then a second of 83 men and 18 women, find refuge with an Aksumite king whom modern historians have alternatively identified with Armah. Many return to Mecca in 622; a second wave goes to Medina in 628.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, The migration(s) and End of the Muslim exile
infobox, lead, The migration(s) and End of the Muslim exile

events.title: Djenné-Djenno settled
events.descr: People first settle the site permanently around 250 BCE (Phase I runs to 50 CE); glass beads there date to as early as the third century BC. A similar settlement at Dia exists from around 900 BCE.

events.title: Eastern Bantu iron-working
events.descr: By the first century BC the Eastern Stream has developed iron forging; by roughly 100 BC to 300 AD Bantu speakers are present at coastal sites such as Misasa in Tanzania and Kwale in Kenya.

events.title: The Bantu expansion reaches South Africa
events.descr: Bantu speakers reach KwaZulu-Natal by 300 AD and Limpopo Province by 500 AD.

events.title: Djenné-Djenno grows
events.descr: The town may cover as much as 100,000 square meters by 400 CE; Phase III runs from about 400 to 900 AD.

events.title: The Arab conquest of Egypt
events.descr: Amr ibn al-As invades in December 639 with some 4,000 men. The Rashidun army wins at Heliopolis on 6 July 640, takes the Babylon Fortress after a siege from September 640 to 6 April 641, and besieges Alexandria from March 641; by September 642 the caliphate has annexed Egypt, Cyrenaica and Tripolitania.

events.title: Celts invade Greece
events.descr: Brennus invades Greece in 281 BC. The La Tène page says Delphi was attacked and sacked in 279 BC; the Galatians page says he was turned back before he could plunder it. Celtic expansion is at its maximum by 275 BC.

events.title: The Galatians settle in Anatolia
events.descr: Celtic settlers come through Thrace under Leogarios and Leonnorios and appear in Asia Minor in 278–277 BC, hired by Nicomedes I of Bithynia. Attalus I of Pergamon defeats them heavily in 240 or 230 BC. Galatia becomes a Roman client state in 64 BC and a province in 25 BC.

events.title: Manlius Vulso’s Galatian War
events.descr: Rome sends Gnaeus Manlius Vulso on an expedition against the Galatians.

events.title: Numantine War
events.descr: A revolt of the Celtiberians of Numantia in Hispania; the first phase ends in 151, and war flares up again in 143. In 134 BC Scipio Aemilianus is sent to end it, and Numantia falls in 133, opening an era of peace in Hispania until the Sertorian War.

events.title: Rome conquers southern Gaul
events.descr: Rome conquers a group of southern Gauls and establishes the province of Transalpine Gaul.

events.title: Cimbrian War
events.descr: Having left the North Sea around 120–115 BC, the Cimbri reach Noricum on the Danube in 113 BC. They invade Gallia Narbonensis in 109 and meet the consul Mallius Maximus and proconsul Caepio at Arausio in 105; Marius is consul five years in a row from 104 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Migrations, Initial defeats, Arausio and Marius
infobox, lead, Migrations, Initial defeats, Arausio and Marius

events.title: Caesar’s Gallic Wars
events.descr: Beginning with the migration of the Helvetii in 58 BC, Caesar resolves to conquer all of Gaul (57), defeats the Veneti at sea (56) and crosses to Britain (55–54). Vercingetorix leads a major revolt in 52. The coming civil war withdraws Caesar’s troops in 50; Gaul becomes a Roman province in 27 BC, but resistance lasts until as late as 70 AD.

events.title: Siege of Alesia
events.descr: In September 52 BC Caesar besieges Vercingetorix, building some 25 miles of fortifications in a month; Vercingetorix surrenders.

events.title: Claudius invades Britain
events.descr: Four legions under Aulus Plautius invade; by 47 AD the Romans hold the lands southeast of the Fosse Way. Caligula had massed 200,000 men at the Channel in 40 AD.

events.title: Boudica’s revolt
events.descr: While the governor Suetonius Paulinus campaigns against Mona, Boudica, queen of the Iceni, leads a revolt; Verulamium burns around 60 AD.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Initial actions and Verulamium
infobox, lead, Initial actions and Verulamium

events.title: Mons Graupius
events.descr: In mid-84 AD Agricola, governor from 77 AD, faces the Caledonians under Calgacus, concluding the forty-year conquest of Britain.

events.title: Hadrian’s Wall
events.descr: Begun in AD 122, in the reign of Hadrian; most of it takes six years to build, by some 15,000 soldiers of three legions. The turf Antonine Wall follows in AD 142.

events.title: The end of Roman rule in Britain
events.descr: The final Roman withdrawal comes around 410 AD; the Anglo-Saxon settlement page gives the traditional end as 411, and the Chronica Gallica of 452 says Britain was ravaged by Saxon invaders in 409 or 410.

events.title: Britain “handed over” to the Saxons
events.descr: The Chronica Gallica of 452 reports for the year 441 that the British provinces have been handed over across a wide area. Gildas, who probably wrote in the early 6th century, is one of the few written accounts of the period.

events.title: Augustine’s mission lands in Kent
events.descr: Sent by Pope Gregory the Great in 596, about forty missionaries arrive in 597; King Æthelberht converts before 601, and by 627 Paulinus has converted King Edwin.

events.title: Battle of the Teutoburg Forest
events.descr: Between 8 and 11 September 9 AD, possibly near Kalkriese; the infobox counts 16,000–20,000 killed. The next major Roman incursion into Germania comes under Marcus Aurelius (r. 161–180).

events.title: Marcomannic Wars
events.descr: After incursions into Raetia and Germania Superior (162–165), thousands of Langobardi and Lacringi cross into Pannonia in late 166, beginning wars that last until 180 under Marcus Aurelius.

events.title: Trajan’s Dacian Wars
events.descr: Discontent with Domitian’s treaty of 89 AD with Decebalus persists, and Trajan reasserts Roman authority. The first war (101–102) ends when Decebalus makes peace; in the second (105–106) the Dacian capital falls and Decebalus kills himself. Southern Dacia is annexed, and Trajan announces 123 days of celebrations.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, First War, Second War and Aftermath
infobox, lead, First War, Second War and Aftermath

events.title: The Salian Franks settle in Toxandria
events.descr: The first known Frankish tribe to settle with official Roman permission. The Franks are probably first named during the crisis of the 3rd century; Constantine executes Frankish prisoners at Trier in 306.

events.title: Alaric I, king of the Visigoths
events.descr: The treaty of 382, after Adrianople, is the first foedus on imperial Roman soil. Alaric, king from 395, sacks Athens in 396 and invades Italy in 401 or 402; he dies at Consentia in 411.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, Early life, Eastern phase and Italy
infobox, Early life, Eastern phase and Italy

events.title: Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the Rhine
events.descr: Traditionally on 31 December 406, near Mainz; Kulikowski argues for 31 December 405. The invaders cross into Spain in September or October 409.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Alternative dating and Aftermath
infobox, lead, Alternative dating and Aftermath

events.title: The Suebi settle in Gallaecia
events.descr: Under Hermeric the Suebi cross into Iberia on 28 September or 12 October 409; in 411 the groups divide Hispania by lot. Rechiar (from 448) is the first Germanic king to profess Nicene Christianity.

events.title: The Visigoths settle in Aquitaine
events.descr: Honorius rewards his Visigothic federates under King Wallia with land in the Garonne valley; with their capital at Toulouse they remain de facto independent, becoming a sovereign state in 475.

events.title: Aetius and the Huns defeat the Burgundians
events.descr: King Gundahar, settled on the west bank of the Rhine since 411, is killed in about 436; in 443 the remaining Burgundians are resettled in Sapaudia.

events.title: The Visigoths annex the Suebi
events.descr: King Leovigild conquers the Suebic kingdom, after campaigns starting in the 570s.

events.title: The Visigoths renounce Arianism
events.descr: Under Reccared (586–601) Catholic Christianity becomes the official religion of the kingdom. The Visigothic Code is completed in 654.

events.title: The Byzantines are expelled from Spain
events.descr: Swinthila ends Byzantine Spania (552–624); by 625 the Visigoths have expelled the Byzantines from Hispania and established a foothold at Ceuta in Africa.

events.title: Theodoric conquers Italy
events.descr: Ordered by Zeno to overthrow Odoacer, Theodoric sets out in the autumn of 488 and wins at the Isonzo (28 August 489), Verona and the Adda (11 August 490). A treaty in February 493 makes Theodoric and Odoacer joint rulers of Italy, and on 15 March Theodoric kills Odoacer at a banquet.

events.title: Reign of Theodoric the Great in Italy
events.descr: King of the Ostrogoths since 471, he rules Italy from Ravenna from 15 March 493 until his death on 30 August 526, and the Visigoths as regent from 511. He visits Rome in 500; Boethius is executed in 524.

events.title: Justinian’s Gothic War
events.descr: The first phase ends with the fall of Ravenna in 540; the second runs from 540/541. In 554 Justinian issues a pragmatic sanction, though some northern cities hold out until 562. The Ostrogothic kingdom ends with Mons Lactarius in 553.

events.title: The Lombards invade Italy
events.descr: In the spring of 568 King Alboin leads the Lombards from Pannonia into Italy. In 572, after Pavia capitulates and becomes the royal capital, Alboin is assassinated.

events.title: Clovis I unites the Franks
events.descr: Clovis succeeds his father Childeric at 15. He defeats Syagrius at Soissons (486) and the Alemanni at Tolbiac (496), and by 509 has united all the Franks and northern Gallo-Romans. Tradition dates his death to 27 November 511; Salic law is first tentatively codified that year.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Background and Middle reign
infobox, lead, Background and Middle reign

events.title: Clovis is baptised
events.descr: He converts to Nicene Christianity rather than Arianism.

events.title: Battle of Vouillé
events.descr: Around spring 507, near Poitiers, Clovis defeats Alaric II, who dies in the battle (allegedly killed by Clovis); the Franks conquer Gallia Aquitania, and the Visigothic capital moves from Toulouse to Barcelona (507–542), then Toledo.

events.title: The Franks conquer Burgundy
events.descr: The Frankish campaign ends near Autun in 534, and Burgundy becomes part of Francia; the Franks extend their rule into Raetia in 537.

events.title: Clotaire II reunites the Frankish realm
events.descr: The realm, divided since Clovis’s death in 511, is reunited under one ruler. Dagobert I, the last powerful Merovingian king, dies in 639.

events.title: Jordanes’s Getica
events.descr: The first written use of the name “Slavs” dates to the 6th century; Jordanes describes them in his Getica (c. 551).

events.title: The Slavs expand west and south
events.descr: Between the sixth and seventh centuries the Slavs expand, reaching the Elbe, the Alps and the Balkans; Carantania is established in the 7th century.

source.sourceLocation: lead ('Between the sixth and seventh centuries')

events.title: The Olmec heartland is abandoned
events.descr: By about 400 BC the major Olmec centres are abandoned; between 400 and 350 BC the population of the eastern heartland drops precipitously. Tres Zapotes continues to be occupied well past 400 BC.

events.title: The Great Pyramid of Cholula begun
events.descr: Its initial stages probably date to the Terminal Formative; its last construction phase is between CE 750 and 950. By volume, 4.45 million cubic meters.

events.title: The earliest Long Count dates
events.descr: Chiapa de Corzo Stela 2 reads 6 December 36 BCE (or 9 October 182 CE), and Tres Zapotes Stela C 1 September 32 BCE, the second oldest Long Count date yet discovered.

sources.sourceLocation: Earliest Long Counts table and Correlations caption
Earliest Long Counts table and Correlations caption

events.title: La Mojarra Stela 1
events.descr: An Isthmian-script text with Long Count dates of 143 and 156 CE, combining images of rulers with script and calendar dates.

events.title: Monte Albán, capital of the Zapotec
events.descr: In the Terminal Formative (Monte Albán II) the city of an estimated 17,200 becomes the capital of a large-scale expansionist polity; by 200 Zapotec influence reaches from Quiotepec in the north to Ocelotepec and Chiltepec in the south.

events.title: The Pyramid of the Sun
events.descr: The largest pyramid at Teotihuacan, whose earliest buildings date to about 200 BCE and whose major monuments are under construction until about 250 CE.

events.title: Xitle erupts: Cuicuilco is buried
events.descr: The city, with some 20,000 people at its peak, is destroyed by the eruption; the lava field covers about 80 km². The eruption may have prompted a mass emigration out of the central valley.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, History and End of the culture

source.sourceLocation: End of the culture ('By the year 400 CE')
End of the culture ('around AD 150 to 200')

sources.sourceLocation: lead, History and End of the culture

events.title: The Temple of the Feathered Serpent is desecrated
events.descr: Power shifts from the temple to the Avenue of the Dead sometime between 250 and 350.

events.title: Teotihuacan at its height
events.descr: In Period III the city of around 100,000 people, about half the population of the Valley of Mexico, has 2,000 buildings over 18 square kilometers; at its zenith, perhaps in the first half of the first millennium, it is the largest city in the Americas. It includes a neighbourhood of ethnic Zapotecs.

events.title: Teotihuacan is sacked and burned
events.descr: Its major monuments are systematically burned; the collapse may be related to the extreme weather of 535–536. The city never regains its population, though it may last until the 7th or 8th century.

events.title: El Mirador at its height
events.descr: The city and its sister centres in the Mirador Basin thrive between 300 BC and the Common Era; major construction at Tikal begins around 400–300 BC.

events.title: The Preclassic Maya collapse
events.descr: El Mirador is abandoned, as are nearly all other major sites in the area, by about 150 AD, after building a large defensive wall. Tikal may have benefited from the collapse.

events.title: Tikal Stela 29
events.descr: The first unequivocally Maya artifact; Stela 46 at El Palmar is said to hold the earliest Long Count of a lowland Maya site (AD 180).

events.title: Siyaj K’ak’ conquers Tikal
events.descr: In January 378 the warlord conquers Tikal; in 378 and 379 he oversees the replacement of the kings of Tikal, Uaxactun and Copán. There is evidence that one of the ruling dynasties of Tikal was founded by conquerors from Teotihuacan.

events.title: K’inich Yax K’uk’ Mo’ founds the Copán dynasty
events.descr: A new dynasty whose founder was probably from Tikal: K’uk’ Mo’ Ajaw is installed on the throne in AD 426, using a title borne a generation earlier by Siyaj K’ak’. He dies between 435 and 437.

events.title: K’uk’ Bahlam I founds the Palenque dynasty
events.descr: He governs for four years from 431.

events.title: Calakmul defeats Tikal
events.descr: A Caracol text says Sky Witness of Calakmul defeated Tikal and sacrificed its king Wak Chan K’awiil. The defeat begins a 130-year hiatus at Tikal and marks the division between the Early and Late Classic.

events.title: Calakmul sacks Palenque
events.descr: Calakmul and its client states attack Palenque in 599 and again in 611; Palenque rebuilds in response.

events.title: K’inich Janaab’ Pakal rules Palenque
events.descr: He comes to the throne at 12, after his mother Sak K’uk’ steps down; he marries Lady Tzakbu Ajaw in 624 and enlarges the Palace in 654, 661 and 668. His Temple of the Inscriptions is begun perhaps as early as 675.

sources.sourceLocation: History, Late Classic and Temple of the Inscriptions
History, Late Classic and Temple of the Inscriptions

events.title: Chavín’s New Temple
events.descr: Built after the Old Temple (c. 900–500 BCE); the culture ends around 250 BCE.

events.title: The Paracas mummy bundles
events.descr: About 420 bodies dating to around 300–200 BCE. Burials at the necropolis of Wari Kayan continue until approximately 250 CE.

events.title: The Nazca Lines
events.descr: The geoglyphs are created between 500 BC and 500 AD, in a Paracas phase (400–200 BC) and a Nazca phase (200 BC – 500 AD). 358 were known by 2022.

events.title: The Huaca del Sol
events.descr: By 450 AD eight stages of construction have been completed on the Moche adobe pyramid, built of over 130 million bricks.

events.title: The Nazca decline
events.descr: From 500 AD the civilization declines, with an El Niño triggering widespread, destructive flooding; by 750 it has fallen completely.

events.title: Tiwanaku grows to significance
events.descr: The city increases its power in the Titicaca basin from 200–500 AD and peaks in 500–600 AD.

events.title: Late Moche: Pampa Grande
events.descr: Late Moche (500–800 AD) is a time of urban nucleation and then collapse; Pampa Grande is prominent in the Moche V period.

sources.sourceLocation: Background and Southern and Northern Moche
Background and Southern and Northern Moche

events.title: Wari expansion
events.descr: The Wari take control of villages in the Carahuarazo Valley around 600 A.D.; the Nazca and Lima pages date the arrival of the Wari in their regions to about 650. From around 600 cycles of drought and El Niño hit the Lima culture.

events.title: Hohokam farming villages
events.descr: Ceramics appear shortly before 300 CE, and crops and agricultural skill increase between 300 and 500. By 600 a distinct Hohokam architecture with Mesoamerican similarities emerges, and agave becomes a major food source.

events.title: Thục Phán founds Âu Lạc
events.descr: King An Dương reportedly annexes Văn Lang; the middle phase of building at his citadel of Cổ Loa falls between roughly 300 and 100 BCE. The infobox also allows a span of 208–179 BCE.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Foundation and Cổ Loa
infobox, lead, Foundation and Cổ Loa

events.title: Zhao Tuo founds Nanyue
events.descr: The Chinese general Zhao Tuo establishes the kingdom at Panyu (now Guangzhou). He first pledges allegiance to the Han in 196 BC, proclaims himself emperor in 183 BC, and rules until 137 BC.

events.title: Nanyue conquers Âu Lạc
events.descr: Zhao Tuo annexes the kingdom of King An Dương.

events.title: Han conquers Nanyue
events.descr: In 113 BC the Nanyue court proposes joining the Han; in 112 BC the opposition kills the Queen Dowager, and Emperor Wu sends 100,000 troops. In 111 BC the Han generals advance on Panyu, and Jiaozhi province is established, beginning the first era of Chinese rule.

events.title: The Trưng sisters’ rebellion
events.descr: In March 40 AD Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị lead the Lạc Việt in rebellion and rule for three years. In 42 AD Emperor Guangwu sends Ma Yuan with 20,000 troops; in the summer of 43 he devastates Jiaozhi and the sisters are defeated.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Biography and Book of the Later Han
infobox, lead, Biography and Book of the Later Han

events.title: Lady Triệu’s revolt
events.descr: The people of Jiaozhi and Jiuzhen rebel against Eastern Wu; after several months of fighting the Wu general Lu Yin puts Lady Triệu to death.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Biography and Modern account
infobox, lead, Biography and Modern account

events.title: Lý Bí founds Vạn Xuân
events.descr: Having revolted against the Liang dynasty with his brother in 543 (541 in the infobox), Lý Bí defeats the Liang, proclaims himself emperor and names the country Vạn Xuân. Liang troops return in 545, and he is assassinated in 547.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Lý Bí and Resistance against the Liang
infobox, lead, Lý Bí and Resistance against the Liang

events.title: The Sui end the Early Lý
events.descr: Having defeated the Chen in 589, the Sui receive the surrender of Lý Phật Tử (r. 571–602).

events.title: Lâm Ấp and the first Cham polities
events.descr: The first Cham polities are established around the 2nd to 3rd centuries AD, in the wake of Khu Liên’s rebellion. The Old Cham Đông Yên Châu inscription dates to around c. 350 AD.

events.title: Roman goods at Óc Eo
events.descr: Funan’s port yields Roman gold medallions from the reign of Antoninus Pius and possibly Marcus Aurelius; Chinese texts claim the Romans first landed in the region before going on into China to conduct diplomacy in 166.

events.title: Chenla takes Funan
events.descr: The Funan infobox gives a Chenla secession in 550 and a Chenla conquest in 627; the Chenla infobox calls 550 vassalage to Funan and 627 independence. Chenla sends an embassy to China in 616/617.

events.title: Isanavarman I founds Isanapura
events.descr: The Chenla capital at Sambor Prei Kuk; a linga inscription there is dated 627 AD.

events.title: Beikthano founded
events.descr: The Pyu begin to enter the Irrawaddy valley in about the 2nd century BCE; Beikthano’s remains date from 200 BCE to 100 CE, and its walls are radiocarbon dated between 180 BCE and 610 CE. Halin is founded in the 1st century AD.

events.title: The Burmese calendar begins
events.descr: The Pyu calendar is launched with an epoch of 22 March 638. Xuanzang (648) and Yijing (675) mention Sri Ksetra.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead and royal names table

events.title: The Tuyuhun kingdom
events.descr: Established by subjugating the Qiang; the people of Murong Shegui cross the Yellow River between 307 and 313, and Tuyuhun dies in 317.

events.title: Namri Songtsen unites the Yarlung clans
events.descr: Around 600 CE he becomes the uncontested leader of the Yarlung clans; he reportedly conquers the Kingdom of Sumpa in the early 7th century and according to Beckwith sends the first diplomatic missions to China in 608 and 609. He is poisoned in 618 (or 629/630).

events.title: Songtsen Gampo founds the Tibetan Empire
events.descr: The 33rd king moves the capital from the Yungbulakang Palace to Lhasa and defeats the Sumpa (c. 627); he is credited with creating the Tibetan script. He dies in 650.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead and History > Songtsen Gampo

events.title: Tang campaigns against the Tuyuhun
events.descr: The Tuyuhun become a vassal of the Tang in 634; in 635–636 Emperor Taizong attacks and defeats them.

events.title: Princess Wencheng marries Songtsen Gampo
events.descr: In 634 Songtsen Gampo sends an envoy to the Tang; in 638 the Tibetans attack Songzhou but withdraw after Tang counterattacks. In 640 the Tang accept his marriage proposal, and the princess leaves for Tibet with Gar Tongtsen.

events.title: The Jokhang
events.descr: Songtsen Gampo builds the temple in Lhasa to house the Jowo Mikyo Dorje.

source.sourceLocation: infobox and History (oldest part built in 652)

events.title: Tibet overruns Zhangzhung
events.descr: Per the Tang Annals, Zhangzhung and various Qiang tribes “altogether submitted” to Songtsen Gampo in 634; R. A. Stein places the conquest in 645. The Zhangzhung infobox gives 625.

events.title: Wang Xizhi’s Orchid Pavilion gathering
events.descr: On 22 April 353 Wang Xizhi hosts 41 friends, relatives and pupils at the Orchid Pavilion on Mount Kuaiji; they compose 41 poems, and his preface, the Lantingji xu, becomes the most famous calligraphic work attributed to him.

events.title: The first Mogao caves at Dunhuang
events.descr: The monk Le Zun has a vision of a thousand Buddhas at the site; the first caves are dug as places of meditation and worship. The earliest surviving decorated caves are built in the Northern Liang period (419–439), and caves continue to be built until the 14th century.

events.title: Faxian’s pilgrimage to India
events.descr: At about 60 he sets out from Chang’an, capital of the Later Qin; he spends ten years in India in the reign of Chandragupta II, leaves from Tamralipti about 409, stays two years in Sri Lanka, and returns in 412 to what is now Nanjing. He writes his travels around 414.

events.title: Kumārajīva translates in Chang’an
events.descr: Born in Kucha in 344 and captured by a warlord in 386, he is brought to Chang’an in 401 under the Later Qin; within a dozen years his translation bureau renders about thirty-five sutras in 294 scrolls. He dies in 413.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Early life, Capture and Arrival
infobox, lead, Early life, Capture and Arrival

events.title: Tao Yuanming retires to his farm
events.descr: The poet (365–427; born 352 by one argument) resigns after some eighty days as magistrate of Pengze and spends the last 22 years of his life on his farmstead.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, Year of birth, Government stints and Return to the fields
infobox, Year of birth, Government stints and Return to the fields

events.title: Liu Yu ends the Eastern Jin: the Liu Song
events.descr: Having led the rising against the usurper Huan Xuan in 404, Liu Yu ends Southern Yan (410) and takes Luoyang (416). On 10 July 420 Emperor Gong of Jin yields the throne to him; he dies on 26 June 422.

events.title: The Reign of Yuanjia
events.descr: Emperor Wen’s reign is known for political stability and capable administration; but he loses three commanderies to the Northern Wei in his first year, his campaigns against Wei fail in 450 and 452, and in 453 his son Liu Shao assassinates him.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and Reign of Emperor Wen
lead and Reign of Emperor Wen

events.title: Zu Chongzhi’s Daming calendar and π
events.descr: At Louxian he compiles the Daming calendar (introduced in 465, with a year of 365.24281481 days) and calculates π as between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927, a precision not surpassed for nearly 900 years.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Life and works and Mathematics
lead, Life and works and Mathematics

events.title: Xiao Daocheng founds the Southern Qi
events.descr: On 3 June 479 he forces Emperor Shun of Liu Song to yield the throne. Sieges and skirmishes with the Northern Wei follow until 481, and peace is signed in 490.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, History and War with Northern Wei
infobox, History and War with Northern Wei

events.title: Emperor Wu of Liang
events.descr: Xiao Yan, a Southern Qi royal and general, takes the throne on 30 April 502. By 517 Buddhist influence is plain in his policies; a Persian embassy brings tribute in 547. He dies on 12 June 549, during Hou Jing’s rebellion.

events.title: The Hou Jing Disturbance
events.descr: The former Eastern Wei general rebels in the summer of 548 and besieges Jiankang that winter; the city falls in 549 (24 April in the Liang infobox). He makes and unmakes emperors, declares himself Emperor of Han on 1 January 552, and, defeated by Xiao Yi’s forces and Chen Baxian, is killed by his own men while fleeing, around 26 May 552.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox and Rebellion against Liang
lead, infobox and Rebellion against Liang

events.title: Western Wei sacks Jiangling
events.descr: The Liang capital falls; Western Wei installs Xiao Cha as emperor of a rump Western Liang at Jiangling, which lasts until the Sui conquer it in 587.

events.title: Chen Baxian founds the Chen
events.descr: On 16 November 557 the former Liang general has Emperor Jing yield the throne to him; he dies in 559.

events.title: Emperor Xiaowen’s reforms
events.descr: The equal-field land system is enacted in 485; in 493–494 the capital moves from Pingcheng to Luoyang; edicts of 495 ban Xianbei clothing and language, and in 496 Xianbei family names are changed to Han ones.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Early personal reign and Late reign
lead, Early personal reign and Late reign

events.title: The imperial caves at Yungang
events.descr: Near Pingcheng (Datong) the first period of carving ends in 465; a second phase under imperial supervision runs from around 471 to 494, when the court moves to Luoyang. Private patronage continues until 525.

events.title: The Longmen Grottoes begun
events.descr: Carving at Luoyang starts with the Northern Wei; the middle Binyang cave is said to have been made between 500 and 523. About 30% of the carvings date from the Northern Wei and 60% from the Tang.

events.title: The Six Garrisons revolt
events.descr: Agrarian rebels overrun the Northern Wei’s northern provinces.

events.title: The Northern Wei splits in two
events.descr: In the fall of 534 Emperor Xiaowu flees west to Yuwen Tai; Gao Huan installs Yuan Shanjian as Eastern Wei emperor (8 November 534), and around the new year 535 Yuwen Tai poisons Xiaowu and enthrones Emperor Wen of Western Wei (18 February 535).

events.title: Battle of Shayuan
events.descr: After the volcanic winter of 536 brings famine to the Guanzhong, Gao Huan launches a major attack on Western Wei in the spring of 537, met at Shayuan; that winter Dugu Xin captures Luoyang.

events.title: Gao Yang founds the Northern Qi
events.descr: Gao Huan’s son deposes Emperor Xiaojing of Eastern Wei; the Northern Qi is established on 9 June 550, with its capital at Yecheng.

events.title: Yuwen Hu founds the Northern Zhou
events.descr: After Yuwen Tai’s death in 556, his nephew Yuwen Hu forces Emperor Gong of Western Wei to yield the throne; the Northern Zhou is established at Chang’an on 15 February 557.

events.title: Northern Zhou conquers the Northern Qi
events.descr: Emperor Wu’s campaign of 576–577 destroys the Northern Qi; its last emperors are captured (28 February 577) and die in late 577.

events.title: Yang Jian takes power: the Sui
events.descr: When Emperor Xuan dies in 580, his father-in-law Yang Jian seizes power as regent; his general Wei Xiaokuan defeats Yuchi Jiong within 68 days. On 4 March 581 Emperor Jing abdicates in his favour.

events.title: Xuanzang’s journey to India
events.descr: He sets out in 629 (627 in another version) and returns to Chang’an in the first month of 645, bringing some 657 Sanskrit texts; his Records of the Western Regions is completed in 646.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Dates, Return to China and Original works
lead, Dates, Return to China and Original works

events.title: The earliest surviving lingling-o
events.descr: Double-headed pendants and earrings carved from nephrite jade. The Maritime Jade Road between the Philippines and Taiwan, established around 2000 BC, peaks until 500 CE and wanes from then until 1000 CE; Philippine craftsmen work Taiwanese jade until around 1000 AD.

events.title: The Sungai Batu brick monument
events.descr: A clay brick monument in the Bujang Valley, described as the oldest man-made structure recorded in Southeast Asia. Sites explored after 2008 are said to date from the 2nd century CE; Ptolemy wrote of the Golden Chersonese.

events.title: Mūlawarman’s yūpa inscriptions
events.descr: Seven stone pillars at Kutai, the earliest known stone inscriptions in Indonesia, whose script is dated to the last half of the 4th century. They name Kudungga, his son Aśwawarman, founder of the dynasty, and his grandson Mūlawarman, but not the kingdom.

source.sourceLocation: Kutai Martapura Kingdom ('last half the 4th century')

events.title: Faxian stays on Java
events.descr: The monk stays on the island of Ye-po-ti, most probably western Java, for six months, from December 412 until May 413.

events.title: Purnawarman’s inscriptions
events.descr: The 5th-century ruler of Tarumanagara produces the earliest known inscriptions in Java. The Ciaruteun boulder, found near Ciampea in 1863, is the earliest to name the kingdom and bears his footprints, likened to Vishnu’s.

events.title: Metal reaches Taiwan
events.descr: Around the beginning of the Common Era, iron and other metals appear and artisans switch from jade to metal, glass and carnelian. By around AD 400, wrought iron is produced locally in bloomeries, possibly a technology from the Philippines.

source.sourceLocation: Metal Age ('around the beginning of the Common Era')

events.title: The long pause in Polynesian settlement
events.descr: Having reached Fiji, Samoa and Tonga by around 900 BC, Polynesians stay at the furthest extent of the Austronesian expansion for some 1,500 years and lose the art of pottery. Around 700 AD they resume their migrations east, to the Cook Islands, French Polynesia and the Marquesas. One cited page, Wikipedia's Polynesians, carries a notice asking for text translated from the Russian article.

events.title: A Melanesian influx into Fiji
events.descr: About a thousand years after the first Austronesian settlers, a large influx of people with mainly Melanesian genetics arrives around the beginning of the Common Era.

source.sourceLocation: lead ('about the time of the beginning of the Common Era')

events.title: Samoa’s unrecorded centuries
events.descr: Little is known about human activity in Samoa in this period, when pottery-making appears to stop suddenly; it may have been a time of mass migrations that led to the settlement of present-day Polynesia.

events.title: Tonga’s Formative Dark Age
events.descr: The population of Tongatapu grows to between 17,000 and 25,000. The Tuʻi Tonga line may begin as early as 950 AD; the maritime empire does not begin until after 1200.

events.title: Early, superseded dates for East Polynesia
events.descr: Older estimates put people in the Marquesas before 100 AD, on Rapa Nui around 300–400 CE and in Hawaii around 300 (Kirch’s textbooks). Recent studies place the Society Islands at about 1025–1120, the rest of the Marquesas at 1190–1290, Hawaii at around 940–1130, and Rapa Nui possibly as late as 1200.

events.title: People on Pohnpei
events.descr: Radiocarbon dating shows human activity at Nan Madol from around AD 80–200; the earliest settlement on Pohnpei was probably around AD 1. Islet building starts by the 8th or 9th century, and the megaliths around 1180.

events.title: A Torres Strait maritime culture
events.descr: The islands are first occupied around 4,000 years ago; by 2,500 years ago more of them are occupied and a distinctive maritime culture has emerged. Agriculture develops on some islands, and villages appear by 700 years ago.

events.title: Dingoes in the Torres Strait
events.descr: The earliest dingo remains in the Torres Strait date to 2,100 years before present; desiccated dingo flesh from Thylacine Hole on the Nullarbor Plain dates to 2,200. The earliest known dingo remains in Australia, from Western Australia, are about 3,450 years old.

events.title: Spear barbs give way to new tools
events.descr: Spear barbs and tips peak about 2,000 years ago, then disappear from the archaeological record in south-eastern Australia, replaced by coastal shell fish hooks and bone points, axes for hunting possums and adzes for digging sticks; regular burning is part of this late Holocene shift. Shell fish hooks appear in Australia about 1,200 years ago.

events.title: Most of Ubirr’s rock paintings
events.descr: The rock faces at Ubirr, in Kakadu National Park, are painted and repainted continuously; most paintings there were created about 2,000 years ago, and some have been repainted into modern times. A painted thylacine shows an animal extinct in the area for about 2,000 years.

events.title: Gautamiputra Satakarni defeats Nahapana
events.descr: Most historians now agree that Gautamiputra and Nahapana were contemporaries and that Gautamiputra defeated Nahapana; the Nashik inscription says he defeated the Shakas (Western Kshatrapas). Scholars date the victory differently: Bhandare to the start of the Saka era (78 CE), Fynes to some time after 71 CE, Dhavalikar to c. 124 CE, which he counts as Gautamiputra’s 18th regnal year. His reign itself is dated anywhere from 60–85 to 106–130 CE.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox and Gautamiputra and Nahapana

events.title: Reign of Toramana
events.descr: King of the Alchon Huns from 493 until his death in 515. His Kura inscription dates to 495–500 and the Sanjeli copper plate to 502–503; Kausambi was probably sacked by his Alkhons in 497–500. The Eran boar inscription is dated to the first year of his reign, placed between 510 and 513. Prakashadharma of Malwa defeats him around 515.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox, Defeats, Sack of Kausambi and Punjab inscription
lead, infobox, Defeats, Sack of Kausambi and Punjab inscription

events.title: Bhanugupta’s Eran inscription
events.descr: An inscription at Eran records that Bhanugupta took part in a battle in 510 CE (Fleet’s 1888 reading); a 1981 translation reads it as a battle against the “Maittras”. The Toramana page says Toramana may have been defeated by Bhanugupta in 510, per this inscription; the new reading removes that link.

sources.sourceLocation: Initial translation (J.F Fleet 1888) and New translation (1981)
Initial translation (J.F Fleet 1888) and New translation (1981)

events.title: Mihirakula rules the Alchon Huns
events.descr: He rules from 515; the Chinese monk Song Yun meets him around 520. His campaign is reversed at Sondani, and Xuanzang says the Gupta king Narasimhagupta Baladitya defeated and captured him.

events.title: Yashodharman defeats Mihirakula at Sondani
events.descr: Yashodharman, and possibly the Gupta emperor Narasimhagupta, defeat a Huna army under Mihirakula and drive the Huns out of India. Yashodharman’s Mandsaur stone inscription is dated 532 AD.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and Mandsaur Pillar inscriptions of Yashodharman

source.sourceLocation: lead ('between 525 and 532 CE, likely by 530 CE')

events.title: Reign of Vima Kadphises
events.descr: Kushan emperor from approximately 113 to 127 CE. The same page also gives 90–100 CE (navbox) and AD 100–127 (a quoted source).

events.title: Vasudeva I, the last great Kushan
events.descr: The last of the “Great Kushans”; his reign extended from at least 191 to 232 CE. He sent tribute to China in 229.

sources.sourceLocation: short description, infobox, lead, Contacts with China and Sassanid invasion in the northwest
short description, infobox, lead, Contacts with China and Sassanid invasion in the northwest

events.title: Shelun takes the title khagan
events.descr: Yujiulü Shelun, crowned 11 March 402, rules the Rouran until 410. He is the first major leader of the steppes to take the title khagan.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox, Reign and Personality and achievements
lead, infobox, Reign and Personality and achievements
lead, infobox, Reign and Personality and achievements

events.title: Peroz I’s wars with the Hephthalites
events.descr: Peroz attacks the Hephthalites in 474 and is ambushed and captured near the border of Gurgan; ransomed, he is defeated and captured again in a second campaign in the late 470s or early 480s, and sends his son Kavad to the Hephthalite court as a hostage in 482. In 484, charging at Akhshunwar’s forces, he and his army fall into a trench and are killed.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox, First and second war with the Hephthalites, Third war with the Hephthalites and death
lead, infobox, First and second war with the Hephthalites, Third war with the Hephthalites and death

events.title: Battle of the Utus
events.descr: A Hunnic victory over the Eastern Roman field armies; Arnegisclus is killed and Marcianople falls. Peace comes with a treaty in the fall of 447 or in 448: 6,000 lbs of gold up front and 2,100 lbs a year.

events.title: Attila invades Italy
events.descr: Attila returns in 452 to renew his claim to Honoria, razes Aquileia and halts at the River Po. Pope Leo I and two envoys meet him at the Mincio near Mantua and obtain his promise to withdraw; Italy had suffered famine in 451, and an East Roman force had crossed the Danube. He dies in the early months of 453.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and Invasion of Italy and death
lead and Invasion of Italy and death

events.title: Battle of Thapsus
events.descr: Caesar defeats the Optimates under Metellus Scipio, with Juba I of Numidia, on 6 April 46 BC (the pre-reform Roman calendar; 7 February by the Julian). Cato commits suicide on news of the defeat, and Juba has a slave kill him after a duel with Petreius. Caesar returns to Rome on 25 July.

events.title: Persia conquers Egypt
events.descr: The Persian invasion begins in 617 or 618; Alexandria is betrayed to the Persians in June 619 (Khuzistan Chronicle), and by 621 the province is securely in Persian hands. Egypt stays Persian for 10 years: in the summer of 629 the Persian troops begin to leave.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox, Fall of Egypt and Aftermath
lead, infobox, Fall of Egypt and Aftermath
lead, infobox, Fall of Egypt and Aftermath

events.title: Marius defeats the Teutons at Aquae Sextiae
events.descr: At Aquae Sextiae (Aix-en-Provence) the Romans under Gaius Marius defeat the Teutons and Ambrones.

events.title: Battle of Vercellae
events.descr: On 30 July 101 BC, near Vercellae in Cisalpine Gaul, Marius and Catulus defeat a Celtic-Germanic confederation under the Cimbric king Boiorix, ending the Cimbrian War.

events.title: Vercingetorix executed
events.descr: Forced to surrender at Alesia in September 52 BC, Vercingetorix is imprisoned in Rome for six years and executed after Caesar’s triumph in 46 BC.

events.title: Germanicus campaigns in Germania
events.descr: Between 14 and 16 Germanicus leads punitive operations against the Germanic tribes, defeating Arminius twice (according to Tacitus), first at Idistaviso. Roman troops recover one of the three lost legionary eagles in 15 and a second in 16. Germanicus dies in Antioch on 10 October 19; Arminius, seeking to become a king, is murdered by opponents in his own tribe in 21.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox and Roman retribution and death

events.title: Battle of Abritus: the Goths kill Decius
events.descr: In the summer of 251 (June, July or August), near Abritus (modern Razgrad) in Moesia Inferior, Goths under Cniva defeat the Roman army; the emperors Decius and his son Herennius Etruscus are both killed.

events.title: The Goths reach the Danube
events.descr: In the summer of 376 a massive number of Goths arrive on the Danube; the Thervings are probably allowed to cross at or near Durostorum. The Gothic War that follows lasts until 382.

events.title: Hengist and Horsa (traditional date)
events.descr: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that in 449 Vortigern invited Hengist and Horsa to Britain to help fight the Picts; the History of the Britons gives 447. Bede records that they were said to have been the first chieftains of the Angles, Saxons and Jutes in England.

sources.sourceLocation: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, History of the Britons and Ecclesiastical History
Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, History of the Britons and Ecclesiastical History

events.title: Battle of Badon
events.descr: A Brittonic victory whose date is unknown. Scholars have proposed 493, 501 and 516; McCarthy and Ó Cróinín revise it to February 482 and Breeze (2020) to 493. Bede’s chronology implies 493–500. Gildas’s account was written c. 543–547.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, Gildas, Bede and Scholarship > Date
infobox, Gildas, Bede and Scholarship > Date

events.title: The Rule of the Dukes
events.descr: An interregnum in the Lombard kingdom (574/5–584/5): after King Cleph dies, the dukes rule without a king for ten years (Paul the Deacon) or twelve (the Origo Gentis Langobardorum). After invading Frankish Provence in 584/5 they elect Cleph’s son Authari king.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Political context, Description by Paul the Deacon and Origo Gentis Langobardorum
lead, Political context, Description by Paul the Deacon and Origo Gentis Langobardorum

events.title: Tikal founds Dos Pilas
events.descr: The Tikal king Kʼinich Muwaan Jol II installs his four-year-old son Bʼalaj Chan Kʼawiil as ruler of Dos Pilas, an offshoot of the Tikal dynasty.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox and 629: Aligned to Tikal
lead, infobox and 629: Aligned to Tikal

events.title: Yuknoom Chʼeen II rules Calakmul
events.descr: He accedes on 1 May 636; his successor takes the throne in 686.

events.title: Dos Pilas becomes a vassal of Calakmul
events.descr: Calakmul attacks and defeats Dos Pilas, which becomes its vassal state; Yuknoom Chʼeen II reinstates Bʼalaj Chan Kʼawiil on its throne as his vassal. (The Yuknoom Chʼeen II page dates his expulsion to 650.)

sources.sourceLocation: lead, 648: Aligned to Calakmul and Known rulers
lead, 648: Aligned to Calakmul and Known rulers

events.title: Bhadravarman I of Champa
events.descr: King of Champa from 380 to 413 and author of several Sanskrit inscriptions; he builds temples and palaces at Mỹ Sơn and Trà Kiệu. He campaigns north in 399 and fights the Chinese governor from 405 to 413.

events.title: Bhrikuti marries Songtsen Gampo
events.descr: A Nepalese princess and the Tibetan king’s first queen, though her historicity is not certain and the date of the marriage is unknown: presumably about the time Narendradeva fled to Tibet (c. 621), or before 624, while one author gives 632.

events.title: Wu Mingche’s northern campaign
events.descr: In spring 573 Emperor Xuan of Chen attacks Northern Qi; by fall Wu Mingche besieges Shouyang, which he captures, and the land between the Yangtze and the Huai is entirely in Chen hands.

events.title: Northern Zhou captures Wu Mingche
events.descr: After Northern Zhou destroys Northern Qi in 577, the Zhou general Wang Gui captures Wu Mingche and some 30,000 foot soldiers on 20 March 578.

events.title: Himiko rules Yamatai
events.descr: The queen of Yamatai sends her first recorded embassy to the Wei court in 238 (Book of Wei; the Nihon Shoki’s quotation gives 239), another in 243, and envoys to Daifang in 247. She dies in 247 or 248.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, infobox, Relations with Wei and conflict with Kuna, Japanese sources, Death and succession

events.title: Empress Suiko; Prince Shōtoku regent
events.descr: Suiko ascends the throne after an assassination in 592 (15 January 593 by the Gregorian calendar, 8 December 592 by the lunar) and reigns until her death in 628. Prince Shōtoku is regent from 593 to 621.

events.title: Golden Age of Athens
events.descr: After the Persian invasion is defeated, Athens leads the Delian League and turns it into an empire whose treasury pays for the Acropolis. Under Pericles the city is home to the playwrights Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, the historians Herodotus and Thucydides, and the philosophers Socrates and Plato.

events.title: Ma'in becomes a kingdom
events.descr: Ma'in, a city-state in the town of Qarnawu in the Jawf, grows into a kingdom: peace with Saba and Saba's defeat of the Nashshan kingdom let the Minaeans extend their power over nearby territories. Inscriptions from the Temple of Shaqab al-Manaṣṣa name many of its kings. One cited page, Wikipedia's Ma'in, carries a notice asking for text translated from the Arabic article.

source.sourceLocation: lead ('transition from a city-state to kingdom in the last quarter of the 7th century BCE')

events.title: Ma'in breaks with Saba and joins Yathill
events.descr: The alliance with Saba breaks down. Ma'in forms a confederation with Yathill (Baraqish) and makes alliances with other South Arabian kingdoms, the basis of its later frankincense trade. One cited page, Wikipedia's Ma'in, carries a notice asking for text translated from the Arabic article.

source.sourceLocation: History ('As the seventh century BCE closed, and the sixth century BCE opened, the alliance with Saba broke down')

events.title: Ma'in absorbs Nashshan
events.descr: Nashshan, the most important city of the Jawf valley, comes under the Kingdom of Ma'in, and Ma'in's pantheon replaces its own; Nashshan restores its old gods when Ma'in falls. One cited page, Wikipedia's Ma'in, carries a notice asking for text translated from the Arabic article.

source.sourceLocation: History ('absorbed under the dominion of the Kingdom of Ma'in between the 6th and 4th centuries BC')

events.title: Minaean caravans outdo Saba's trade
events.descr: By the middle of the 1st millennium BCE, Ma'in's trade in aromatics surpasses Saba's, and it takes over the caravan route along the Red Sea. Its caravans reach Egypt, the Levant, Mesopotamia and Greece; about seventy Minaic inscriptions mark its trading communities abroad, most at al-Ula, and one at Delos records an altar to its god Wadd. One cited page, Wikipedia's Ma'in, carries a notice asking for text translated from the Arabic article.

source.sourceLocation: International trade ('The Ma'in trade surpassed that of the Saba by the mid-1st millennium BCE')

events.title: Vedic religion develops into Brahmanism
events.descr: The late Vedic religion develops into Brahmanism, centred on the Ganges basin.

events.title: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad

events.descr: In the Book of Nehemiah's account, the scribe Ezra reads the Mosaic Torah to the people of Judea; Julius Wellhausen dated Judaism as a religion of Torah law from this reading.

events.title: The sun cult of Ra rises to dominance
events.descr: In the Old Kingdom the sun god Ra becomes the chief god of the pantheon, and his solar cult gains power.
